When we have reached the com-mitteee stage questions may be put, but when the House is sitting as such and the Prime Minister or the leader of the opposition addresses the Chair he should not be subjected to these interruptions; it is not fair.
Mr. Speaker,-
Order, order.

I am addressing my words to Mr. Speaker, whose observations were particularly directed to me. I merely wanted some information which was not given by the Prime Minister. I did not intend to be impertinent, nor did I expect an impertinent reply.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
No one thinks the hon.
gentleman was impertinent; he never is, and could not be. But- I say it is not proper that the Prime Minister or any other hon. member who has the floor in a budget debate should be constantly interrupted in this way. It is turning his speech into a cross-examination, which is not fair to the hon. member who addresses the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to proceed. I will now give the total number of persons on the pay rolls of thirty-seven manufacturers of agricultural implements, as shown in the re-
turns made to the statistical branch of the government. On April 1, 1922, there were 5,205; April 1, 1923, 6,580; April 1, 1924, 6,176; April 1, 1925, 5,793, and on April 1, 1926, 8,257. That shows the extent to which working men were thrown on the streets and driven out of the country. At the time the right hon. leader of the opposition made that statement, April 1, 1924, there were 6,176 persons on the pay rolls of these thirty-seven manufacturers of agricultural implements. On April 1 of this year there were, not 6,176, but 8,257; so much for the effect of the changes in the tariff. Now I would like to come to this year, as an indication of how matters are now prospering. On January 1 of this year 7,084 persons were employed in the manufacture of agriculture implements; on February 1, 7,494; March 1, 7,859, and on April 1, 8,257. I have no doubt that during the rest of the year we will find the number increasing, for the reason that the business itself is not only prospering within this country, but in competition with foreign nations as well.
That is the next point I wish to come to. We were told that we were ruining industry and sending people out of the country, but what do we find? We find not only that conditions have improved with respect to domestic sales but that, as a matter of fact, in the export of agricultural implements there has been an increase of very material proportions. Let me read the values of the exports of farm implements and machinery by years:
1921-22		
1922-23		
1923-24		
1924-25		
1925-26		
In 1924-25, after our budget changes were made, the exports amounted to 111,342,712 and for the complete twelve months of 192528, $13,628,341. In other words, from the time the change was made the exports increased from $9,330,519 to $13,628,341. These are the facts which may be cited in reply to the assertions made at the time as to what the effect of the government's action would be. If more is needed to make clear the position of the implement manufacturers I would quote for just a moment from the reports of one or two of these companies. We find that so far as the implement manufacturing business is concerned, the companies are beginning to pay dividends, for practically the first time in their history, and that not only on preferred stock but on common stock as well in some instances. I have here the report of the Cockshutt Plow Company, appearing in the Financial Post of February 19, 1926. I

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
will not read the whole of the report, but just one or two statements:
The annual report of the Cockshutt Plow Company for 1925 shows profits from operation after providing for depreciation of $313,501, compared with $64,347 in 1924.
That is what the report of this year shows. The vice president of the company, outlining the position of the industry, said:
Referring to the year's operations and the outlook, vice-president F. Perry says:
The improvement is encouraging, and it is to be hoped that prices of agricultural products are emerging permanently from the depression in relation to other prices into which they have been sunk since the war. The success of the company's business, he says, is directly dependent on the prosperity of the farmers. While business in eastern Canada has also improved, the increase was by no means so marked as in the western provinces. Foreign sales, however, have reached a higher figure than in any previous year.
Collections, on the whole, have been good, and the shorter terms of credit which were introduced some time back are now beginning to show a beneficial effect in the reduction of the amount of dealers' and farmers' paper carried by the company, and a corresponding reduction in the company's borrowings from its banker. On December 31, the company's bank loan was entirely paid up, and its trade liabilities reduced to a minimum.
That the company is now in a position to take advantage of improved conditions, including the Russian orders for tractors which have been received, has been reflected in the action of the market and the substantial advance in the quotations for the shares of this company.
That is a pretty good record for two years; improving business in eastern Canada; increases even more marked in the west; foreign sales reaching a higher figure than in any previous year; collections good; reductions in the company's borrowings from its banker; trade liabilities reduced to a minimum, and substantial advance in quotations for shares. What more could you possibly wish for any industry anywhere?
Now take another great company, namely the Massey-Harris. The report of that company appears in the Financial Post of February 12 of this year, and is headed as follows: Massey-Harris Company. A great Canadian industry which stands second in its field in world trade. Big improvement in business is now being experienced.
The article goes on to say:
Speaking of the farm implement industry in general and of the Massey-Harris Company in particular, Thomas Bradshaw, general manager of the company referred to, states that the implement business is in a better position to-day than it has been since 1920. Sales during 1925, especially in the home market, increased considerably	Mr. Bradshaw estimates
that farm equipment sales in Canada during 1925 were from 60 per cent .to 75 per cent in excess in 1924.
There is a statement which has a direct bearing upon the motor industry at the moment.	I said a little while ago that the
moment the country knew that the question
of duties had been settled, purchases immediately began to be made. I would like to read that sentence again:
Mr. Bradshaw estimates that farm equipment sales in Canada during 1925 were from 60 per cent to 75 per cent in excess of those in 1924.
I contend that that is very largely to be accounted for by the fact that many farmers were waiting until the question of the tariff was settled, and until they were in the best position to make purchases. The article goes on to say:
Exports likewise showed a healthy increase. Farm implements were exported to practically every grain growing country of the world, with Great Britain, France, Germany, Russia, New Zealand, Australia, Argentina and the United States as their chief destination.
As to 1926, the prospects are for still further improvement in the implement industry. The demand for goods should he greater and plants more fully occupied. Mr. Bradsihaw makes the point that perhaps never before has the feeling between the implement manufacturer and the farmer been so harmonious.
I will just add this further statement as to the company's report for the year ending November 13 last:
The company's report for the year ending November 30th last, showed net income of $2,346,543, compared with $1,065,180 for 1924, while an addition there was $661,139 .made available by recovery of assets previously written off. This indicates a splendid recovery of the company's affairs. A few years ago the company owed its bankers a sum between $12,000,000 and $13,000,000, representing implements sold on credit. Not only has this debt been liquidated, but recently the company has been able to show a substantial cash surplus.
May I add this further word? After it became apparent that the agricultural implement industry was going to improve, we were told that it was not so much the implement industry that hon. gentlemen opposite were concerned about as it was some subsidiary industries from which raw material had to be obtained, and particular mention was made of the steel industry. Now what is the position of the steel industry, a manur facturer of parts of agricultural implements? The Financial Post of December 11, 1925, has an article headed:
Steel of Canada crosses par for first time since merger organized in 1911. Investment history made as well-managed steel enterprise makes good visions and promises of promoters oif pre-war days.
Here is the paragraph that bears on the point:	'
This week the common stock of Steel Company of Canada sold over par for the first time in its history. This event is of importance for investors because it indicates that the public is now beginning to recognize Steel of Canada as one of the basic securities of Canada, a security that is bound to reflect business conditions in general and that may, in
3484	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
time, be regarded as a barometer of Canadian business just as United States Steel is regarded as a barometer of business in the United States.
Then within the past month the Financial Post, which keeps track of these matters, has two further references to the financial position of these implement companies, one on May 14 referring to the Cockshutt Plow Company.
It is being credited that dividends will be increased on Cockshutt shares before the end of the year, probably at 4 per cent.
The item with respect to the Massey-Harris Company says:
The preferred issue is now regarded as being on a sound dividend basis, with good prospects for a moderate dividend on the common in the not far distant future.
There, Mr. Speaker, in a word is the answer to the assertions made by hon. gentlemen opposite as to the effect of the government's reduction of customs duties on the implements of agriculture. At that time the government stated that it felt secure in the action which it was taking, that it believed the result of the changes being made would not only be of assistance to the farming community, but would prove beneficial to the companies as well. In every particular the position taken by the government at that time has been implemented to the full. Now I venture to say, Sir, when we are permitted to consider a couple of years hence the effect of the changes we are making to-day in the duties on automobiles, we shall find this whole situation with relation to agricultural implements paralleled' in all the particulars I have mentioned' with respect to the motor industry in Canada.
May I say just a word about the manufacturing industry as a whole in this country? To hear hon. gentlemen opposite talk, one would think they were the only persons concerned about the well-being of manufacturing in Canada, and they never cease to stress the point that manufacturing in Canada is suffering under this administration.
Mr. BENNETT, Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend says, "hear, hear.'' I want this noted, because it bears out how much reliance one can place on "hear hears" or statements of the kind that are made. I want to bring this point to the attention of my hon. friend who has just interrupted, and he may be surprised to know it. Will he be surprised if I tell him that this year for the first time in the history of this country our exports of manufactured goods exceed our imports?
It is mostly paper and that class of raw material.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is exports of fully manufactured goods.
Paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Paper may be imported' too, if my hon. friend insists on thinking only of paper. Let me give to the House statistics that cannot be controverted as to our exports and imports of manufactured goods.
Mr- BENNETT: Our imports would be steel, principally. We are the second customer of the United States in steel.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Not in 1921. If my hon. friend wants to take a war year, or any year where-we have not got stagnation in the buying countries, he would not take 1921.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That was a post-war year, in which a number of contracts were being carried on, and the total export of manufactured goods in 1921 amounted to $665,087,939. The year following is the proper one with which to begin making com-

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
parisons. There is disclosed a steady increase in exports. I would like hon. gentlemen opposite and the House to get the significance of the figures presented in this table. Let me give the excess of imports over exports or the excess of exports over imports for the different years. In 1921 the excess of imports over exports was in round figures $264,000,000; in 1922, that had dropped to $120,000,000; in 1923, it had dropped to $59,000,000; in
1924,	it had dropped to $47,000,000; but in
1925,	the exports exceeded the imports by $15,000,000. There is the proof that manufacturers in Canada have prospered under this administration. Consider for a moment the significance of those figures.
Under the late government, the official statistics show that the Canadian market was on balance invaded by imported manufactured goods to the tune of $264,000,000, or considerably more than a quarter of a billion, in 1921. This government, they say, has been pursuing a policy of tariff reduction inimical to the interests of our manufacturing industries, yet in each succeeding year the manufacturers of Canada, taken as a whole, clearly have more and more occupied the home market, if we balance the exports against the imports of manufactured commodities. Finally, after our 1924 budget, which the opposition declared was going to ruin the Canadian manufacturers, our manufacturers, taken as a whole, won out on balance against their competitors from abroad, and exported $15,000,000 more manufactured goods to other countries than other countries sent to Canada. This showing will undoubtedly be better in 1926, in view of our enormous favourable balance of total trade, but apart from that, the table shows conclusively that under the present government, Canadian manufacturers are more than holding their own, not only in the markets of Canada, but in the markets of the world. The record shows dearly that the great body of Canadian manufacturers are more completely holding the Canadian market than they were four or five years ago. The facts given in the table are a complete refutation of the blue ruin utterances of the opposition.
May I give one other brief reference which I think will be illuminating as to the manufacturing industries of this country and the state of Canadian trade. Hon. gentlemen opposite are continually comparing conditions in Canada with conditions in the United States to the detriment of their own country. They cannot deny that; they are continually doing it in their public utterances, and yet the available statistics disclose that instead of there being reason to belittle our country there
is the strongest reason in the world why we should make it plain to everybody that we are in a much better position than our neighbours to the south.
In that case why are our people going to the United States?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They continue to go, in so far as they may be going, because of the propaganda in which hon. gentlemen opposite indulge.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I venture to say that of the people who have left Canada for the United States more have done so in consequence of the talk of hon. gentlemen opposite than 'because of any other reason. I go further and I say that in addition to this fact it is also true that thousands of people who otherwise would have come to Canada, have been led to locate in other countries because of the utterances of hon. gentlemen opposite. My hon. friends seem to delight in keeping up a propaganda aimed at depreciating Canada; they seem to delight in deriding and belittling their own country-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Slandering it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, "Zander" is not too strong an expression to use. Such conduct as that cannot be indulged in without having very serious effects upon this country. Now, this policy of belittling Canada is shown to be without justification when one considers the total trade of the Dominion, that is the import and export trade and realizes that for the year ending March, 1926, there was a favourable trade balance of $401,134,000. That is a figure that has never been reached before in the history of this country, excepting possibly, when munitions of war were being exported. Even the United States, notwithstanding the immense trade which it enjoys, does not begin to have as favourable a trade balance as Canada enjoyed for the last fiscal year. In proof of that may I offer the following figures. For the twelve months ending March, 1926, the visible trade balance of Canada amounted to $401,134,000, and that for the United States to $352,364,000. Recently published figures of the United States bringing its trade statistics down to the end of March show that for the first nine months of its fiscal year ending June its favourable trade balance or excess of exports over imports was $187,000,000. Adding to that figure the favourable trade balance of the United States for the three months, April, May and June of last year, namely, $165,000,000, we find that the total favourable trade balance of the United States for the period included in the last Canadian fiscal year was $352,000,000, or a cool $50,000,000 less than our favourable trade balance in the same period. This fact is a remarkable demonstration of how' Canada is holding her own in the markets of the world. The policy of the present administration, of cheapening the instruments of production, has operated to increase the volume of Canadian exports.
Will the right hon. gentleman be good enough to give us the trade balance between Canada and the United States for the same period?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are trading with the world.

The trade
balance between the two? I have not the figures here, I am sorry to say. In what I have said to-day and I must apologize if I have taken up an undue amount of time, I have endeavoured to show that the blue ruin representations in which hon. gentlemen opposite have indulged are not justified by the facts, but that as a matter of correct record this country has really gone steadily ahead in the manufacturing industry, not only absolutely in its own accord but relatively in comparison with its neighbour and chief competitor.
I should like to say something further with respect to some of the features in the budget. During the course of this debate so much has been said about the need for protection and the like, which is not borne out by the facts, that I am afraid the House and possibly the country have lost sight of the budget itself and what it discloses-what it discloses of improved conditions in our own country, and what it promises of reduction in taxation to the people. If it may be permitted I should like to say a few words on that aspect of the question and therefore as this is a convenient point of departure, Mr. Speaker, I ask that you call it six o'clock.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. R. J. Manion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the course
of my remarks during the afternoon, referring to the fact that hon. members opposite failed, in the last parliament during the course of any debate on the budget, to move an amendment declaratory of their professed advocacy of protection, I omitted to make mention of one incident to which I had intended to refer, but which helps to illustrate the truth of what I was seeking to have the House appreciate, namely that the hon. members in one way or another contrived to avoid a full discussion of the question of protection which would place the House in relation thereto definitely on record in any budget debate. The point that I overlooked referring to-I had it before me but overlooked it- was the circumstance that on the eve of the assembling of parliament at its last session there appeared in the Ottawa papers and other papers throughout the country a statement in the nature of a manifesto of the Conservative party in respect to its views on protection, and when the House assembled members discovered that this manifesto was in the form of a resolution on the order paper in the name of the right hon. leader of the opposition. That resolution did contain in it a statement that:
This Dominion requires an immediate revision of the Canadian tariff, on a definitely and consistently protective basis.
That resolution appeared on the order paper on February 5, 1925. It remained there day after day, but was never taken up in the course of the debates in the House. It remained there, I would like to point out to

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
the House, through the whole of the discussions on the budget. If the right hon. leader of the opposition and members of his party had been really anxious to test the feeling of the House on a declaration of that kind, that was the appropriate time to do it. As a matter of fact the debate on the budget last year lasted altogether, I think, forty days and forty nights, the longest debate that ever took place in this House on any single question. During all that time this motion of the right hon. leader of the opposition remained on the order paper. It continued on the order paper until about the end of the session. I think, to be exact, it was on June 2 that this resolution was moved as an amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply. It was on the order paper until the day before, and a good many hon. members were taken by surprise when they found it had been withdrawn from the order paper and was being introduced as an amendment to the motion to go into supply. However, the House had had enough of discussion on the tariff question and dealt pretty summarily with this motion. It was debated a few hours, I think, and ifinally was disposed of on division, by a vote of 147 to 37. In other words a majority of 110. in the House as then constituted, voted against a resolution declaring that this country required an immediate revision of the Canadian tariff on a definitely and consistently protective basis. The interesting fact in regard to the debate that took place on that resolution was that not only every Liberal member of the House of Commons, but every Progressive member, the Labour members, the Independent members, and the only lady member in the House, voted against it. It was virtually on this resolution that hon. members opposite conducted the recent campaign.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon.
friend says, "Hear, hear". I believe he is following me in this debate. And yet we come to the first session of the new parliament and that resolution is entirely discarded, and instead of having anything declaratory in regard to the necessity for an immediate revision of the Canadian tariff on a definitely and consistently protective basis, we have the resolution now before us dealing with a matter of procedure.
Hon, members opposite have sometimes expressed surprise that, in view of their campaign last election, and in view of the fact that as a party they were returned with the
largest number, they should not be sitting on this side of the House conducting the affairs of the country. Let me say to the House frankly that after the election of October last, when I called to confer with His Excellency on the question as to what course should be followed as a. result of the situation that had been created by that election, I took the position that in my opinion the right hon. leader of hon. gentlemen opposite could not command the support of a majority in this House of Commons, and I took that position largely because of this resolution which had been defeated in the House by a majority of 110 in the previous parliament, and by reason of the attitude which hon. gentlemen themselves had assumed during the campaign when they told the people that the one great issue, so far as they were .concerned, was the tariff. I said quite frankly that I did not see how members of the Progressive party, or of the Labour party or independent members of the House, any more than members of the Liberal party could endorse the fiscal policy of the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). I was prepared however to leave it entirely to the House of Commons itself to declare its views on the matter, and I think hon. gentlemen will credit me with having endeavoured in every possible way to allow that expression of opinion on the part of parliament to be altogether unprejudiced and untrammelled. The House of Commons did declare itself on the question of majority support, as it will be called upon again to-night to declare itself; and I would say, in all seriousness, to my hon. friends opposite that after parliament has recorded its vote, upon the conclusion of this debate to-night, the country will take little stock in further references to the alleged inability of the government to function or to the assertion which has been so strenuously put forward, that the government has no right to continue in office.
I said that I desired to offer a few remarks regarding the budget itself and to remind hon. members, before they came to cast their votes, just what the budget discloses and what is proposed in the resolutions which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) will move in due course. In the first place, Mr. Speaker, may I take this occasion to join with others who have spoken on both sides in extending heartiest congratulations to the minister on the budget which he has been able to bring down as a consequence of the financial position in which the country finds itself to-day? If he has succeeded, as I believe he has, in presenting to this House what
3488	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
is unquestionably a more popular budget than any that has ever before been submitted to parliament, a budget that means more in the way of reduction in taxation than any other which it has been the good fortune of this country to receive, the credit cannot be too largely attributed to the minister himself, for the manner in which he has presided over the finances of the country, the great caution and care he has exercised with respect to expenditures, and the eminently capable way in which he has furthered the financial policies which this government has deemed most in the interests of Canada.
The minister last year in presenting his budget said that he wished to err on the safe side. He preferred to over-estimate any expenditures that might be made, and to underestimate the revenues of the country. He came to parliament this year and was able to show that as a matter of fact that was what he had done; the surplus of last year was shown to be greater than he had assumed it would be when he made his statement to parliament. I am sure hon. members will be pleased to learn that the Minister of Finance has followed the same cautious course at this session. In presenting his budget a month ago he underestimated the revenues of the country for the last fiscal year while he overestimated public expenditures, with the result that the surpluses which we have to declare to the country to-day are very much greater than were anticipated when the 'budget was brought down last month. Fortunately we are now in a position to submit the complete statement for the last fiscal year and the facts disclosed therein will, I am sure, be received by the country with the greatest satisfaction. The minister estimated in his budget statement that the increase in revenue would be $29,965,520; as a matter of fact, it is $32,900,000 odd. He also over-estimated expenditures, for, as the facts now show, the surplus of revenue over expenditure instead of being $55,000,000 odd, as the minister stated then, is $58,404,060, while the surplus over ordinary and capital expenditure instead of being $38,065,000 is $41,594,000. The surplus on government services is also higher than the minister had predicted: Instead of being $33,910,000 as he estimated it is $37,526,000. The net public debt on March 31 my hon. friend estimated would be $2,395,000,000 odd; as a matter of fact it is considerably lower than that, being $2,391,000,000. The public debt reduction during the past year, instead of being $22,353,000, as the Minister of Finance anticipated, is $25,969,000, or very nearly $26,000,000.
These are some of the features of the budget which the Minister of Finance has presented

to parliament and the country on this occasion, but there are other aspects of the situation which are equally noteworthy. He pointed out that through the management of the finances under his direction the bonded indebtedness of the country had been very much reduced. The bonds held in the United States have been paid off in part, while the rate of interest which we were obliged to meet on bonds has been considerably lowered, by the refunding of loans effected. An appreciable saving has been effected in that way. With respect to the Canadian National Railways the minister was able to report that instead of the railways being any longer a liability they are rapidly becoming a national asset. In addition to that he was able to report progress in the right direction so far as the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is concerned. He was able to point out that through the removal of the cattle embargo, brought about under the present administration, the number and the value of cattle being exported from Canada to the British market had largely increased, while he was able to make the gratifying announcement that trade through Canadian ports had made material progress. The hon. member who spoke this afternoon (Mr. Macdougall) observed that the trade coming through Maritime ports under the British preference was almost within one per cent of 100 per cent, and he credited the government with arranging to include that extra one per cent. What he failed to notice, however,- possibly he may not have been aware of the fact-is that the reason the 99 per cent of that trade is coming through Canadian ports is to be found in the action taken by this government three years ago providing that on the trade coming through our ports a discount of 10 per cent on existing customs duties under the British preference would be allowed, the effect of that policy having been to divert practically the whole of the trade enjoying the preference.	1
In addition to these unmistakable and unquestionable evidences of the growing prosperity of the country the Minister of Finance was able to announce to the House a reduction in taxation in many directions. In the first place there was the reduction in taxation in customs duties on automobiles, motor trucks and motorcycles, then the reductions in income tax, certain reductions in the sales tax, and the abolition of the receipt tax. Then, too, there was the announcement of the return to the penny postage. These are all a part of the budget which the minister has presented to the House and which hon. members will be asked later on to declare themselves upon as

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
either favouring or rejecting. I think it is well that these points should be emphasized, because hon. members are apt to lose sight of them in the course of a long debate such as we have had on this occasion. May I, by way of further confirmation of what I have already said, draw the attention of the House to the fact that the earnings of the Canadian National Railways for the calendar year 1925 will show an excess over all operating and income charges of S30,433.852.	But the figures have
since come in with respect to the other three months of the present year, so that the fuli return is now available for the fiscal year 1925-26. This will show earnings in excess of operating and income charges, not of $30,443,000 but of $38,000,000.
I have already spoken of the favourable balances of trade which have been referred to by the Minister of Finance. Our favourable balance of trade now stands at $401,000,000 odd. This is an increase in our export trade during the year of $247,000,000. The favourable balance this year has increased from $284,000,000 to the $401,000,000 already mentioned. Of this increase no less than $104,000,000, or 90 per cent, is accounted for by trade within the empire. Hon. gentlemen opposite sometimes assert that the government has effected little by its policies. I am seeking not to indulge in generalities but rather to give to the House concrete and exact evidence with respect to our achievements.
One of the important strokes of policy which the government effected, and which previous governments had failed to bring about, was the removal of the British cattle embargo.

the time. It was unquestionably due to the efforts of our High Commissioner, the Hon. Peter C. Larkin, supported by the present administration, that that embargo was removed after we came into power. Let me give the House a statement of the effect of the removal of that embargo on April 1, 1923. For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1923- to give the figures before the removal-25,758 head of cattle, valued at $2,809,796, had gone into Great Britain. In 1924, after the removal of the embargo, our exportations of cattle to Great Britain had increased to 59,486 head, valued at $6,287,815. In the next year, 1925, that
business had increased to 86,245 head, valued at $9,125,667. This last fiscal year ending March 31, 1926, instead of the 25,758 head of cattle that went into the British market before the embargo was removed, 117,819 head were landed there at a valuation, not of $2,800,000 odd, but of $12,432,954.
Now a word in regard to the reduction in taxation. As hon. members know, in addition to the miscellaneous small, changes to meet growing conditions, there is a reduction of the tariff duty on automobiles valued at not more than $1,200 and on motor trucks and motorcycles from 22^, 30 and 35 per cent to 12i, 17) and 20 per cent, while on automobiles valued at more than $1,200 the tariff duty is reduced from 30, 32 and 35 per cent to 15, 25 and 27) per cent, being the British preferential, the intermediate and the general tariff respectively. I quote these figures that hon. members may have clearly in mind the extent of the reduction in duties that has been made.
In regard to the income tax, the Minister of Finance was able not only to announce a reduction, as he described it, "all along the line," but he was also able' to inform the House that the act is now being presented in a less complicated form than heretofore, and that the reductions which he was proposing -this is something that I believe has never been paralleled before-would take effect during this present year, on the incomes of the year just concluded. From one end of the country to the other there is scarcely a home which does not appreciate the fact that it has less to pay out in taxation to the federal treasury than was the case a year ago. To emphasize the importance of the reductions effected, Mr. Speaker, let me cite a few specific instances. On an income of $3,000 the tax was $40; that income is now completely exempt. On an income of $6,000 the tax was $178.50; it will now be $70. On an income of $12,000 the tax was $871.50; it will now be $460. On an income of $18,000 the tax was $1,753.50; that has been reduced to $1,210. There can be no denying the saving which these reductions mean to individuals, to business interests and to future investments in this country. But in order that hon. gentlemen may see that the government's exemptions extend even further than what I have indicated, may I remind the House that in previous budgets the government granted certain exemptions based on the number of children in a family and increased these exemptions on one or two occasions.
The hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) the other evening, referring to the income tax, pointed out that there seemed

What he failed to recognize was that the exemptions I have referred to were reaching out in the directions which it was hoped they might; that is, that large numbers of families which were formerly obliged to pay income tax were now exempt. Under the present budget a man with an income of $4,500 and a wife and three children is entirely exempt, but in 1921, when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office, he had to pay $76, and last year he contributed to the treasury $40. There is a showing, Sir, which I think will be appreciated by every family in the Dominion.
I omitted to mention that there are also certain sales tax exemptions on a number of articles; that on canned1 fish for example, the sales tax has been reduced from 5 per cent to 24 per cent; I did mention that the receipt tax has been completely abolished; and that penny postage will come into force again after July 1 of the present year. Altogether my hon. friend estimates that by his budget he is relieving the people of $25,000,000 of taxation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wi^h to quote two paragraphs from the speech which my hon. friend made when introducing his budget and to ask the House for a moment to consider seriously their significance. He had drawn attention to the fact that great as are the exemptions in taxation which he was prepared to ask the House to make at the present time, he believed1 they would have been greater still, and that our prosperity would have been still more pronounced, if some of the citizens of the Dominion, rather than knocking conditions in this country, had instead been doing something in the way of boosting them. This is what my hon. friend said in that regard:
The Canadian people, in poping with the era of depression which followed'iThe collapse of the postwar boom, have been unnecessarily hampered by a plague of gloom which shrouded the thoughts and utterances of too many Canadians, and but for which the prosperity of the moment would be even greater than it is to-day my privilege to record.
But he closed with this optimistic note, which is the other side of the picture:
This era of depression has been overcome:	all
statistical compilations which mirror the year to year business of Canada prove it. Canada to-day is steadily growing more prosperous; there is less unemployment; the influx of settlers is growing; and with a hopeful spirit manifesting itself throughout Canada from coast to coast, the year 1920 is full of promise.

Now listen to the statement in regard to the Canadian National Railways and see how true it sounds. This statement was made at the same time.
If they-
That is, the members of the present administration.

I venture the assertion, Mr. Speaker, that language of that sort cannot be exceeded. Hyperbole is a figure of speech, but this goes far beyond hyperbole.
With this statement on the one hand, which I think I am justified in characterizing as a picture of gloom, let us take the facts on the other side, facts which cannot be controverted, with respect to the actual prosperity of the country. Here I would like to quote from sources which I think my hon. friends opposite will agree are authentic. -I take first of all the statement of the Royal Bank of

The generally favourable annual reports issued by the leading Canadian corporations, combined with the excellent position of all statistical indices, and a general increase in the volume of forward buying, indicate a more encouraging outlook for Canadian business in 1926 that at any time in the past five years.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just one word about the significance of the figures which I have just quoted and in particular as to the significance of the reduction in taxation which has been effected by the present budget. That reduction in taxation is due to the policies of this administration, persistently and consistently pursued during the last four years.
When this government came into office it was confronted with a very difficult situation. We started out to try to meet that situation by introducing policies which we hoped would further production, would lead to wider markets, would !be of service to industry generally, and we also sought in a very drastic way to reduce public expenditures so that we could cut down taxation. Now we have succeeded in reducing expenditures to a very considerable degree. But hon. gentlemen opposite, being possessed of the habit of criticising not fairly, but rather of saying anything which might be detrimental to the present administration, have even during the course of the present debate undertaken to say that this government has not cut down expenditures. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who was acting as financial critic in the absence of the hon. member for West York, made a very positive statement in that regard, a statement which was followed, I notice, by one or two others who spoke after him. At page 2459 of the Hansard of April 15th, he is reported as saying:
So that the government year by year is progressing on an ascending scale in the matter of national expenditures.
He is also reported as saying:
On the other hand, in the public services of Canada, there has been year by year under this government an annual increase in our expenditure. I make that statement without fear of contradiction.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I say that statement is contradicted by all the official records and the facts that we have; I say that without any fear of contradiction. In charity to my hon. friend who made the statement, I must say that he came into the breach rather

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
quickly and did his best to meet the obligation customarily assumed by the hon. member for West York, who is the regular financial critic of the opposition, and I think he must unintentionally or unwittingly have made the statement that he did.
iHon. gentlemen may say that we are referring to one set of figures while they are referring to another. There are three comparable sets of figures so far as expenditure is concerned. There is, first of all, the total expenditure of the country, including everything-the grand total. In the second place, there is the expenditure which is the ordinary expenditure so classified, together with the expenditure on capital and special accounts. That leaves out of account any expenditure in the way of advances to the Canadian National Railway or to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. Finally, there is the ordinary expenditure so classified in the public accounts of the country. Now I say without any possibility of being contradicted from official sources, if you take any one of these three groups of comparable expenditures, you will find that there is not a time since this government came into office up until the present moment when the expenditure has not been reduced every year, year by year, excepting this last year, where there is a slight increase that I shall account for in just a moment-a slight increase which, when explained, will help to show to the House that the record which the government has been making in reducing the expenditure has been kept up all along the line.
Perhaps I may explain at once what the additional expenditure is that has increased the total somewhat. Last year there was an expenditure for the general election of about a million and a half dollars; I shall give the exact figure later. That was an expenditure of an exceptional character. It cannot properly be regarded as indicating any lack of effort on the part of the administration to continue reducing the expenditure.
But there was another item which was very much larger, and that is the amount paid by the government to the Home Bank depositors, which is an exceptional expenditure and which cannot be considered as coming within the ordinary expenses of government.
In the third place, there was considerable increased expenditure incurred in payment of pensions to the returned veterans, due to the policy which the government adopted of permitting appeals to a pensions board. A considerable amount of increased expenditure was incurred on that account. These three
items together will account for from one to two times the difference that exists between the expenditure of this and of the previous year. Now, may I make this assertion, which I challenge any hon. gentleman opposite to correct? It is that the difference between the grand total expenditure to-day and the expenditure in 1921-22-and in that year we had only been in office three months- amounts to $107,000,000. That represents the difference this year as compared with the expenditure in 1921-22. But if the comparison is made with the year 1920-21 when the right hon. leader of the opposition was in office, the difference will be found to be $170,000,000 instead of $107,000,000. In other words during these two years $277,000,000 in the way of additional expenditures were added to the obligations of this country over and above our rate of expenditure in the fiscal year 192526. Now if we have succeeded in bringing down taxation in the way we have it has been due to the fact that we have consistently and persistently pursued a policy of reduction in expenditure.
There is one other observation I would like to make. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that we have increased taxes. The statement was made by an hon. gentleman (Mr: Macdougall), who spoke this afternoon. He said the sales tax during the period his leader was in office, and before, was less than it was after we came into power-that we added to the sales tax and some other taxes. Why were these additional taxes imposed? It was 'because of the financial situation that had developed under hon. gentlemen opposite which was bringing this country to a state of ruin and bankruptcy and which had to be stopped at all costs. Hon. gentlemen opposite when in office-and this is apart altogether from war expenditure,- went on increasing the total expenditure of the country at a very considerable figure. But they did not meet that additional expenditure by taxation, they met it out of borrowing. Now every dollar borrowed means so much in the way of future taxation, and all the money hon. gentlemen opposite borrowed during those years to meet current expenditures instead of raising it by taxation is properly chargeable to themselves rather than to this administration by way of taxation. When we got into office what did we find? We found that the credit of this country had depreciated to a point that the country had to pay seven per cent interest at New York to finance the very best securities, government guaranteed securities of the Canadian National Railways, and we found the dollar worth only 82 and 83 cents.

speechtext:
I should not wish to refer anything unless I referred the whole of it. But let me go a step further. Not only is what I have said about the capital cost of the war quite correct, but hon. members, in placing this colossal mortgage on the back of the country-because that is what it is

increasing thereby the interest on the public debt that has to be carried year by year, made it more difficult for subsequent governments to collect taxation to help to meet that great obligation. They issued a large proportion of their bonds tax exempt. When they were carrying on the finances of this country by issuing tax exempt bonds and were increasing the public debt of this country in that way they were laying up an obligation which subsequent governments had to meet and which we had to face. That is why we had to put on extra taxation-because hon. gentlemen opposite had borrowed instead of taxed and robbed us of the opportunity of getting in the form of income tax what we should have had and what any government should have had as a source of revenue.
I am taking more time than I should, but it is better that the country should know the exact facts, and I think hon. members will acquit me of the charge of having taken up too much of the time of the House this session. I certainly did not take up much of the time during the first month. Let me supplement what I have just said by an accurate statement of the figures. I will deal with the revenue from taxation only, since that revenue constitutes the real binder upon the taxpayers of Canada. The revenue raised in the pre-war fiscal year ended 1914, after hon. members opposite had been in office three or four years, amounted to $126,143,275, or $16.40 per head of officially estimated population. In 1911, when hon. members opposite came into office, the revenue from taxation was not $126,000,000 but $88,000,000 odd, or $12.31 per head of population, instead of $16.40, showing that as soon as my hon. friends came into office they began to increase the expenditures Of the country. In 1915 the revenue from taxation amounted to $97,000,000 odd, or $12.40 per head of the population. In 1916 the revenue from taxation was $124,000,000 or $15.51 per head of the population. Those were war years. Hon. members will notice that less was raised in taxation during the war years than was raised in taxation in 1914, the year before the war commenced; at a time when the financing should have led to increased taxation, less taxation was being imposed. Then in the year 1921 the government raised from taxation the sum of $368,-
770,498, but they added to the national debt $92,000,000, a process which implies future taxation. If they had sought to balance the budget as we have sought to do, they would have had to raise $460,780,858. In 1922 the revenue from taxation was $319,926,013, but they added to the national debt 881,256,817. To balance the accounts for the year they would have had to raise $401,182,830. It was this ruinous and spendthrift course which in two years added $173,000,000 to the national debt, more than one-half the total pre-war debt of Canada. This had to be stopped, and that is what this government sought to do. We set out to do it first of all by seeking to cut down expenditure and by introducing policies which would lead to increased production. In 1923 we raised in taxation $335,453,431. That was not enough to balance the budget and we were forced to add to the national debt $31,641,067, but that was the last addition we made to the national debt; since that time we have been reducing the national debt rapidly. In the three latest fiscal years combined, 1924, 1925 and 1926, this government raised by taxation in the aggregate $962,913,325, but at the same time we wiped out the national debt to the extent of $62,308,183. The current taxes of the country during the three years were something like $900,600,000, on the basis of a tax revenue of about $300,000,000 per annum. Yet those who in 1921 imposed on the people in current taxation $368,770,498 and in future taxation $92,010,360, or a total of $460,980,858, and in the year 1922 in current taxation, $319,926,013 and future taxation $81,256,817, making a total of $401,182,830, have such short memories that they now accuse us of excessive taxation.
With the permission of the House I desire to place on Hansard a carefully prepared comparative table showing taxation necessary to balance the budget, actual total taxation and consequent addition or subtraction to the public debt. The statement covers the years from 1921 to 1926, both inclusive, and shows that in 1921 there was added to the public debt over and above taxation levied the sum of $92,000,000 odd. In 1922 there was an addition of $81,000,000 and in 1923, $31,000,000. In 1924. 1925 and 1926 there were subtractions of $36,000,000; $345,000; and $26,000,000 respectively. In other words, there was a saving to the taxpayer in present taxation or future taxation arising out of debt of over $100,000,000 as compared with 1922, and over $160,000,000 as compared with 1921.

You will recollect that Peel had been the leader of the Conservative party, and later he introduced a measure which resulted in the repeal of the Corn Laws, although he had appealed to the people for support to retain them. Mr. Disraeli, as he then was, attacked Peel and pointed out that such a course robbed parliament of its reputation and destroyed the honour of the institutions they were sworn to protect. During the course of his observations on one Occasion Mr. Peel made some reference to Mr. Canning, whom he had not treated very well. Let this country and this House be under no misapprehension. When the right hon. gentleman came into power the debt of this country was as I have indicated, 
and to-day it is greater. What interest have we in income and expenditure if at the end of the period of time the obligations of this country, apart altogether from its indirect obligations with respect to the railways, are more than they then were? Let there be no misunderstanding in that respect; these are the facts.
I do not propose to go into the question of income and expenditure except to point out that in the year 1920-21 the government of the day determined that at all hazards it would balance the budget. You will observe that for the first time in the history of Canada the government then collected more than $400,000,000 in revenue. That will be found at page 45 of the Public Accounts, the exact figure being $436,292,184.41. In 1922, in consequence of certain remissions of taxation, that was reduced to $382,000,000, but in the year in which this government had full control, in 1923, it exacted from the people $403,000,000, and the next year $406,000,000, so that of the three times in the history of this country in which over $400,000,000 was extracted by way of taxation from the people of this country, two of them were occasions on which the taxes were imposed by the government of the right hon. gentleman opposite. My right hon. friend has claimed great credit to the administration for having created what he called wider markets. Wider markets for whom? Will any hon. gentleman opposite deny that every trade treaty that has been negotiated by this administration since it came into power has resulted in increasing the trade of that country with us and decreasing the trade of this country with them? Wider markets? The United States, in their official bulletin issued in November, 1924, pointed out that every revision of the tariff in this country under the present government had been a revision downward, and that the effect of revising it downward had been to increase the trade in manufactured goods of the people of the United States with Canada, with a corresponding loss to our manufacturers in this country. Talk about your treaty with the West Indies, or about your treaty with France or Italy or Australia. The cold-blooded facts are these: We have increased the trade these countries have done with us, but we have lessened the trade we have done with them. That is the position. Hon. gentlemen opposite get up and tell this House that this government is widening markets in this country. Of course, you are widening them; you are widening them for our competitors, for those countries who are sending out commercial agents to every part of the world. You are widening them for the United States, increasing the sale of their products to us, and diminishing our sales to them, with corresponding loss of work for our own people. So much for that.
Then, arising out of that matter, my right hon. friend referred to the great reductions that had been made in the duties on agricultural implements, and to the decrease in prices with respect to them. That, he pointed out, is a wonderful thing accomplished for this country. But, Sir, I will point out that the prices of implements in western Canada at least are not any less than they were before this tariff was reduced if you deduct the sales tax and adjust your prices accordingly. What happened? Let us look this thing fairly in the eye. A colleague of the right hon. gentleman whom an informed electorate rejected in Durham cried almost in tears when the government reduced the duty on agricultural implements, and further, if the right hon. gentleman will induce Mr. Massey to withdraw the privilege that he attached to a letter he wrote to the right hon. leader of this opposition, so that the letter may be given to the people of this country, we shall have a clear understanding of what he thought of those reductions in the tariff. Why, Sir, what happened then? Mr. Massey, the president, and Mr. Bradshaw journeyed to this city when the duty was being removed, and told the government of the day what the situation was. Ruin staring them in the face, they said; workmen who had been with them for years thrown out of work. And the government did what? It took off the sales tax, and it made free the materials that they use in the manufacture of their machines. That is what the government did. And the Massey-Harris Company is better off to-day and actually is enjoying higher protection than ever before. I warn my friends to the left-Beware 1 The government that yielded to the importunities of Mr. Massey, the government that put upon the free list all the materials that are used in the manufacture of implements, the government that did these things is now playing with this automobile tariff, and the people of this country who have been made to believe that this government is going to strike a blow at protection will find out before very long that the automobile industry will have a higher rate of protection than it ever had.

You looked as though you would like to. Let me proceed a step further. What has been the result in Nova Scotia? The two great factors that are to be considered in the manufacture of implements are steel ingots and pig iron. Do you realize what the position of this country was before the right hon. gentleman passed his tariff and put these materials on the free list? I have in my hand the figures with respect to the iron industry taken from the Iron Age, with which I am sure most hon. gentlemen are familiar and you will observe that the way in which they compute is from an index number. They take 100 as representing the monthly average production of pig iron in 1913 in the United States and Canada. In 1914 the figure stood at 69 for Canada and 75 for the United States.
I will skip the years 1915 and 1916 when production went up, and will come to 1919, In that year the figure in the United States was 100 and in Canada 81. The next year the figure went up to 120 in the United States and in Canada to 96. In 1921 it was 54 in the United States and 60 in Canada. In 1922 the figure was 87 in the United States; in Canada it had shrunk to 38. In 1923 the figure in the United States was 130 and in Canada 87. In 1924 when this beautiful scheme devised to please Mr. Massey became effective I find that in the United States the relative number was 101 and in Canada it was 59. In 1925 it was 118 in the United States and in Canada 58. I have the various months right down to 1926. We find that in January of this year the figure was 130 in the United States, and that was 30 over par. In Canada the figure was 68 or 32 under par. In February the figure in the United States was 114, or 14 over par as against a figure in Canada of 60, or 40 under par. In the month of March the figure in Canada was 64. The figures in the United States for that month have not been compiled, but they were over par. That is what happened. We have an 
industry on the verge of bankruptcy, one of the very greatest industries that ever can be established in this country. Protection has been taken from it and as a result the United States blast furnaces and steel mills are running to capacity, while the Nova Scotia mills are being ruined and are on the verge of bankruptcy. These are facts from which there is no escape. It is pointed out that the result of this has been to remit $3,000,000 to the Canadian farmers, representing the sum which it is asserted the Massey-Harris Company unjustly extorted from the people of this country, nevertheless that same Mr. Massey is chosen as a leader in Israel and the colleague of the right hon. the Prime Minister.
Then I turn to steel ingots, and I find the same position relatively. Starting with the index number of 100 I come down to the year 1924 and I find that in the United States the number was 122 and in Canada 62. In 1925 the number was 146 in the United States and 72 in Canada. And if you take the record month by month you will find this is what happened: Just as soon as these materials were placed upon the free list just as soon as Canadian development stopped, just as soon as the tariff was remitted against the importations for these purposes, our production lessened. The index number in the month of June in the United States was 81 and in Canada 79, only two below. In July the number was 74 in the United States and 60 in Canada; in August 101 in the United States and 26 in Canada; in September 112 in the United States and 21 in Canada; in October 123 in the United States and 23 in Canada; in November 123 in United States and 26 in Canada; in December 141 in United States and 30 in Canada. We have 3teel ingots in January of this year in the United States at 165 or 65 over par; in Canada down to 79. In February the number was 150 in the United States and 61 in Canada. In March it was 165 in United States and 68 in Canada. There is the tale.

Furthermore, paints and varnishes, materials that go to furnish employment for Canadians, are coming in free, and tending to reduce the number of people working in the agricultural implement industry in Canada. I point out that the number of these employees, greater though it is now than in 1921, is thousands less than it was in 1919. In the factory which the Massey-Harris Company owns at Batavia they are making more money than ever today, and this money is going into the exchequer of the Canadian company. But in order to accomplish that result manufacturing is being carried on in the American plant; the Canadian plant is becoming a mere assembling plant for American materials. They manufacture in their factories in the United States and buy in the open market the materials required for manufacturing purposes which are used in their factories in this country. These materials are shipped across to Canada and assembled here. That is the story with respect to the effort to reduce the duties on agricultural implements.	The price of
agricultural implements has not been reduced except to the extent of the sales tax. What has happened is that injury has been done to that great enterprise, the agricultural implement manufacturing business in Canada, to say nothing of the injury resulting from the destruction of our iron and steel industry, the lessened demand for Canadian paints and varnishes and all those other materials that enter into the manufacture of the finished product.
But that is not all. The right hon. Prime Minister stated a moment ago-I do not know what, induced him to do it-that the right hon. leader of the opposition had pointed out that the result was going to be tremendously injurious to Canada.. At column 2106 of volume 3 of the debates of parliament for 1924 I find these words from the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen:
Now I am going to make a few remarks on the present changes.
That was after the King government had swept away the sales tax and made various changes in the duty.
They embrace reductions on agricultural implements; reductions, however, far more serious in the case of those other manufactured .products which enter into the construction of such implements; reductions as well in mining and logging machinery. There is a reduction in implements of some four per cent on the main items, five per cent on some others, and as high as even ten per cent. Reductions are given however on what are called raw materials but what are really manufactured materials produced by other supplying plants. The importation of these materials is allowed virtually free, wholly free in so far as pig iron and steel are concerned, and almost free as respects all
other commodities. Just what the effect is to be on the agricultural implement industry I do not undertake to say; time will tell. I do not presume that very great change is made as respects that single industry; but the .penalty is heaped on others in order that hon. gentlemen to my left may be enticed.
Those were the words of the right hon. gentleman. He did not for a single moment raise a blue ruin cry or that the changes in the tariff would mean destruction to the industry. He said that he could not say just what the result would be, but he added: You strike at the whole fabric of protection, you destroy these smaller industries that are supplying component parts to the larger industries, and you are giving employment to thousands of workmen in foreign lands that they may be able to partly manufacture or partly process goods that are sent into this country to be completed and afterwards sold to the Canadian people. That is what has happened in the case of the agricultural implement industry. The manufacturing is carried on in the plant at Batavia. The plant at Toronto has become more and more an assembling plant. Let us look these facts squarely in the face; let us be under no misapprehension with respect to the situation. That is what is being done in the case of one of our greatest industries. In the United States it is said that steel is king. That means that the steel industry is so important to the people that there is a direct relation between the prosperity of the steel industry and the prosperity of the country as a whole. And in the United States to-day you will find the prosperity of the steel industry reflected in the prosperity of the people themselves.
But in this country the pig iron

National unity! While with one hand destroying our industries and with the other giving our raw materials to the manufacturers of the United States and permitting them to come in here with their finished products. That is what they call national unity. National unity in their dealings with the Maritime provinces which have made such a contribution to the country with their vast resources! Do hon. gentlemen realize that the people of the great republic to the south of us regard those deposits which are capable of making pig iron and steel as

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
case of all these partly processed materials, has not the time come for us to consider what our exports mean to us? Then there is a point that should never be lost sight of when we are shipping out of the country these vast quantities of pulp and paper, namely that we are denuding our lands of their forests .and, vihat is more, destroying capital that cannot be replaced. This is a serious matter. What is the reason our friends from the United States come here and establish industries? Because Canada is the greatest depository of raw material now available on the continent. Should we not therefore carefully ponder the situation and try to understand why it is that other countries are preserving their forests while we are allowing ours to be exploited to our very serious disadvantage? These are questions that call imperatively for consideration. When I say that the major part of our exports consists of the two items I have mentioned, let me add that it looks as though the limit will soon have been reached so far as our exports of wheat are concerned. This is a grave matter and one that is of vital moment to the country from which I come. The limit of the absorbing power of the purchasing countries of the world to which we ship our wheat and cereals is nearly reached; how nearly I do not know, but I do know that from an analysis of the figures made by men in the trade it is quite clear that with the effort being made to stimulate the production in European countries, and with the possible come-back of Russia at no distant date, we have nearly attained the maximum so far as our exports of grain in Western Canada are concerned. If that be so, then at once there arises a question of the first magnitude which demands the serious consideration of the government. I mention this in passing, because it must be clear that in Great Britain, France, Germany, Spain and other countries a most determined effort is being made to-day to do all that can be done to stimulate production and to obviate as far as possible any reliance upon other peoples for food supplies. The effect of shipping out all this grain rather than manufacturing it into flour in our own country, and the present condition whereby the foreigner gets the benefit of these exports to the extent he does, is reflected in the invisible claims that are made upon us. I will not argue this point to-night, but I may tell the Prime Minister that if only he will look closely into it he will be forced to a conclusion wholly different from the one he has expressed.
