Again, with Mr. Gladstone, I decline to prescribe until I am called in. So much for immigration and trade, and so much for the public debt.
Now let me consider questions more immediately dealt with in the budget. One of these is the income tax reduction and the reduction in the duty on automobiles. The Prime Minister this afternoon challenged the opposition in reference to its amendment, and rather questioned the sincerity of the motion. He suggested that the amendment did not ring true to the principles the opposition espoused and the principles it enunciated during the election. He added that at least during this session we had not endeavoured to indicate our reliance upon the maintenance of a general protective policy in this country. I find by reference to Votes and Proceedings No. 17, at page 58, that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) moved in amendment to the Speech from the Throne the following motion:
That the following words be added to the said Address:
"We desire respectfully to express regret that the Speech from the Throne gives no indication of policy designed to enlarge the volume of employment in Canada, and particularly to give to the producers of farm products, coal and other primary products the advantage they are, under present world conditions, entitled to enjoy in the market of this country."
Could anything be clearer than that? I will admit that my right hon. friend at that time was inadvertently absent from the Jlouse, but at any rate the fact is that the journals of this House show that by this amendment the party on this side of the House asked for protection. The amendment was negatived by a vote, I think, of 115 to 125.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend that nothing could be clearer than that the word "protection" does not appear in the amendment?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know it is quite unnecessary to use the word "protection" to carry its meaning to the right hon. gentle-

The Budcjet-Mr. Bennett
man. In England, for instance, it is called what? The safeguarding of industry. We desire that Canadians should have an equal opportunity to work out their destiny and develop the resources of their country. You may not use the word "protection", but the only method by which you can secure that growth of trade, by which you can safeguard the industrial life of this country, is by the adoption and the maintenance of a uniform principle of protection. It is perfectly true that the word "protection" is not there, and yet every speech made upon that amendment was a plea to the government to embark upon a policy of defined and maintained protection. Those speeches were made alike by members from Ontario and from British Columbia, by members representing the fruit growers of Nova Scotia and the lumbermen of New Brunswick, by members representing the artisans in the industrial centres, by members representing all walks of life and all trades-they made speeches upon that amendment in which they pleaded for the safeguarding of the industrial and agricultural life of this country, for the protection of the fruit industry and the vegetable industry from the encroachment of our neighbours, in order that we might be able to bring back those 500,000 people from the States, and, bringing them back, to keep them in this country. The greatest problem that confronts Canadian men of thought and vision to-day is to keep in this country' the people we have here and to add to their number. That, Sir, can be done in one way, and one way only-by giving our men and women work to do. You cannot give them that work unless you protect them against the unfair mass production of their richer and more powerful neighbours.
Let us go a step further and look at what happened with respect to our balance of trade with the United States. My hon. friend referred to the balance of trade in this country. I am getting away from the main line of my argument, but I left out something a moment ago, and my remarks must necessarily be disjointed because I did not have any time to collect information while my right hon. friend was speaking. What happened? Last year we sold to the United States $474,890,000 worth of goods, and we bought from them $609,820,000 worth. And as was pointed out in official documents issued by the government of the United States, our tariff reductions have meant an increasing demand in this country for their manufactured goods. The result is that that balance of trade adverse to us represents over $100,000,000 in money that we gave to our powerful
mass-producing neighbours to the south and that we could have spent at home in making Canadian goods. Until that fact is ground into the hearts and minds of the Canadian people and they realize it- as I believe they are beginning to-and until a government sits on the treasury benches which will give effect to that principle, the movement of our people south will continue. It is bound to. It is simply the attraction of the large body for the small. The great industrial hive of Montreal is affected by it. Ontario, our foremost province industrially, has felt it as no other province has. This afternoon my friend referred to what had taken place in the city of Branford. The best answer to that is the absence from this House of the member who formerly represented the city of Brantford. I am sure my friend was wrong in what he said respecting the Cockshutt Plow Company. They are going to make a first payment on the arrears of their preferred dividends, not on their common stock. And according to the record in the Secretary of State's office the Massey-Harris Company recently underwent a recapitalization by which its 250,000 shares were converted into 125,000 preference and 125,000 common-very greatly, it is alleged, to the detriment of some of the smaller shareholders; a matter about which I express no opinion, being without any knowledge respecting it. But I think my friend must be entirely mistaken if he assumes for a moment that industrial activity in Canada is spelling any form of prosperity for those engaged in it, for reasons which I shall presently point out.
I was proceeding to discuss the question of the reduction of duty on automobiles, upon which the right hon. Prime Minister laid a great deal of stress. It is a perennial subject; it was discussed in this House last session and the session before. I ask hon. members to bear with me while I point out two or three observations that I think worthy of their attention. I ask the House for a moment to look at what transpired in the course of the debate upon this subject. I find that the same motion made last year was again moved this year, and I notice that the Minister of Finance on that occasion made some very pertinent observations. He said:
If his statement to-night is correct it would seem that there has been some United States capital invested in the business since then. But without going into that feature, I would remind the hon. gentleman that no matter where the capital comes from, the industry gives employment to Canadian labour. There are 78 plants engaged in the manufacture of automobiles and their accessories in Canada, employing Canadian labour,



The Budget-Mr. Bennett
and subject to Canadian taxation, a considerable amount in taxes finding its way into the Canadian treasury.
He went further, he added:
I submit to hon. gentlemen that the automobile is a fair source from which to collect revenue.
As I said in opening it is on the eve of the budget, and the government must have revenue from some source. Demands come to the government from those who desire expenditure for new railways, the extension of existing railways, harbour improvements, bridges, grain elevators and other public works-these alternating with requests that we part with various sources of our revenue. If we are to meet our national obligations-the interest on the national debt, the pensions that we owe to our soldiers and the widows and orphans of those who will never come back, and the cost of administration, we must have revenue from some source, and if you take away the revenue we are getting from automobiles we must secure it by imposing duties upon some other commodity.
I ask my friends to the left to keep that in mind. Rejoicing though you are to-day on the reduction of the duty on automobiles, remember what the Minister of Finance said on that occasion-and he is still holding that portfolio-that if the duty on automobiles was lessened he would have to get the revenue from some other source. He is not getting it this year; he is going to fool us and get it next year. That is the position. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) in the course of some observations said that a 10 per cent reduction in duty might be reasonable on the lower priced cars, leaving the duty unchanged on the higher priced cars. Then the vote was taken on March 16, 1925. This is an interesting matter. The House, unable to get more detailed knowledge with respect to this matter, having in fact no detailed knowledge, groping in the dark, some members believing the duty too high and some believing it to be too low, and all desiring to receive further knowledge, were implored by the Minister of Finance to wait until the budget came down. That was what he pleaded for. The right hon. Prime Minister this afternoon said that the Conservative party in caucus assembled had not dared to frame a resolution with respect to automobiles. He also said that the reason the government had not proceeded with the tariff commission in advance of the budget was because they were unable to get the gentlemen they desired and therefore had to deal with the matter before it could be referred to the commission. I will tell the House why this reduction in the automobile tariff took place. It did not take place because they could not refer it to the tariff commission; it did not take place because the Progressives alone wanted it; it took place because those who supported it could not trust the Prime Minister and wait for the budget. They did
LMr. Bennett.l
that last year and were deceived, so they insisted on it this year. That is what happened, if hon. gentlemen would like to know, and I venture to say that the Minister of Finance was not any too strong on incorporating the reduction in the automobile duty into his budget without a reference to the tariff commission.
The Prime Minister referred to what took place in the Conservative caucus. So far as I know the matter was not discussed, but there are rumours which seem to be fairly well founded, in view of what happened, that those from Saskatchewan and Quebec and other parts of Canada who desired a reduction in the automobile duty said, "We will not wait for the budget; we were asked to wait last year and nothing happened; we are taking no chances this year, but we will insist upon it in the budget itself," and that is the reason it is there.
Now let us go a step further. The right hon. Prime Minister this afternoon gave as a reason for not'submitting this to the tariff board the fact that he had not time to do it before the matter had to be dealt with in the budget. Let us look at the facts. I find the Minister of Finance reported in the Montreal Gazette of October 13, 1925, as having said:
We say that neither those who ask higher tariffs, nor those who ask lower tariffs should be ignored, but we do say that before ruling for or against either, a case must be made out, and proof given to a board of competent advisers. . . .
Then I find that the right hon. Prime Minister used practically the same words, only in his case he promised to have a woman on the board. He said:
If someone comes from the prairies and says we sell in a free trade market and buy in a protected market and ask for a policy of free trade, no government could do it, because it would create discontent in Ontario and Quebec. Similarly if a group of men came from these provinces and asked the government to shut out outside goods by a high protective tariff, could a government listen to that?
He says they could not do so, and then continues:
We are not a cabinet of supermen,-
That is news.
-but we can get together men who are experts. We have decided to form a board to consider all tariff schedules, and to call for advice to the board representatives of manufacturing, of commerce, of agriculture, of labour, and also of the women, so that the homes would be dealt with fairiy. We will consider the tariff with the advice of this board.
That is what the Prime Minister said when seeking the support of the electors of this country. Then again, speaking in Montreal, he said:

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
The government believed that since many technical matters were involved it was well that there should be formed a body composed of the experts in the government's service, with an advisory board of representatives of the various interests, and including a woman, who would study tariff matters, and whose recommendations would be brought to the study of the cabinet. He did not believe the government should seek to be arbitrary or be governed by dogma in such a matter.
In the city of Quebec he repeated the same thing.
That board would be above partisan appeal or sectional interest. It would study the situation on its merits and its recommendations would be made to parliament direct. . . .
Then further:
It was his intention also to see that a woman was named because he thought it only meet and proper that the growing importance of women's interests in the life and work of the nation should be given the recognition it deserved.
I could read more of the same thing but, Mr. Speaker, as in many other matters of this character, the Prime Minister has seen fit to forget his promises and has remembered only the power which he has attained by making these pledges and then repudiating them.
There was a distinct promise to the electors of this country that there would be a tariff board. The Conservative party promised the same thing in the speech made by my right hon. leader in 1925.' Not only was a tariff commission promised, but one in which the evidence would be open to the public, in order that the public might have the fullest information with respect to changes in the tariff. That was the promise given by the Conservative party. We realize, as every man in this House must realize, how difficult it is to understand fully the complex operations of the tariff, and to come to an adequate and proper conclusion with respect to how far-reaching its ramifications may be. For instance, during the recent election I told the electors of the constituency in which I live, that, in my private opinion, the tariff on automobiles was higher than it should be, but I said I did not pretend to be able to speak with authority because I had not the requisite or necessary knowledge. But I said I knew that the party to which I belong had pledged itself, if returned to power, to obtain the appointment of a board to receive the evidence and place it before parliament in order that its recommendations might be understood fully in the light of all the evidence adduced, and in order that parliament might arrive at proper conclusions. What happened? The people realized that that was so; they believed the statements made by this government when they said that was what they proposed to do. This govern-14011-223J
ment promised the tariff board before parliament met, and when parliament assembled the Speech from the Throne indicated that a tariff board would be appointed.
This afternoon my hon. friend pointed out that the words "not before" were used in the amendment, but I point out to him that the Speech from the Throne contains stronger words than those. It says that changes in the tariff should be made "only" after the fullest examination of their bearing upon both primary and manufacturing industries, and that representations requesting increase qr decrease of duties should be made the subject of the most careful investigation and report by a body possessing the qualifications to advise the ministry with respect thereto. "A tariff advisory board will accordingly be appointed forthwith." You will notice that it says "only"-

speechtext: After investigation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Surely, by an advisory
board. That investigation has not -been made because tihe board was not appointed, it is said, in time to conduct it.
Now let us go a step further. Surely my right hon. friend knows that in the United States there exists a similar advisory board. He also knows that when the first tariff was passed after the Republican party last came into power a duty of 30 cents was imposed against Canadian wheat. Then, when the new tariff was prepared, the duty was increased to 35 cents, and the fanners of the western states said it was not high enough. What happened? An investigation was held in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and -as a result of that investigation the President increased the duty to 42 cents. There was no necessity to call -congress together to do that. I wonder if anyone in this House thinks for a moment, or if this country will be deluded into the belief, that this government could not have passed legislation to reduce the duty on automobiles without calling parliament? Is anyone fooled by that sort of cant, or deluded by that talk? What was done when we reduced the duty on wheat? An order in council was passed reducing the duty on American wheat, and automatically our wheat went there free. How is it done in England? After an investigation has been made it is carried out by parliament in some instances, and in others it is not. This country -could have passed legislation by which power would have been given the Governor in Council to reduce the duty on automobiles if the investigation held by the advisory board so warranted. That is the position.
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

speechtext:
Not unless the legislation so provides. II pointed out that existing legislation does not confer that power upon the Governor in Council, and my hon. friend chose cottons in order that he might strike terror, I suppose, into the heart of some people whom he is very anxious to placate, and has always been very desirous of doing so. It is something he understands fairly well. It was very astute of him to suggest cottons, but I do not think it will have the desired effect. If this parliament so desires, it can do what has been done in the United States. I have the statute under my hand. The Governor in Council could be clothed with the same powers as the president of the United States, and upon a report made to the Governor in Council, upon the evidence being submitted, the government could either increase or reduce the duties if they so desired. That is the point I desired to make, and I desire to make it abundantly clear that any excuse given for breach of faith, for breaking a solemn promise made by the represents-
IVIt. Bennett.]
tive of the sovereign in this country, is wholly without warrant and without merit in view of the use of the word "only."

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does my hon. friend advocate that we should follow that policy?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My right hon. friend this afternoon said that we were simply raising a matter of preeedure. That reminds me of tire story of the Irishman who was condemned to death, that being the penalty fixed by the statute for his offence, and he complained that he was being hanged merely as a matter of form. I am not advocating any course. I am giving the answer which must be in the mind of every man to the paltry excuse given by the Prime Minister, that we could not have this board function because it was not appointed in time. Anybody knows that if the necessary legislation had been desired, the thing could have and would have been done; the legislation could have been passed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon.
member, or does the Conservative party advocate that such legislation be passed?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have pointed out to
the Minister of Finance that it was not the function of an opposition, in answering the statement made by the Prime Minister, in answering the excuse he gave-which was absolutely without merit-for not referring this matter to a tariff board, to state what one would do. But I say this: If the Conservative government had been in power, it would have neither increased nor reduced the duties without first referring the matter to the tariff commission as had been promised.
I put this to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). He has farmers in his constituency upon whose homes mortgages are being foreclosed, I am sorry to say. That is going on in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. If the mortgagee made a promise by which he said, "I will not foreclose your mortgage until next year. I will leave the matter in abeyance until then, and will not take any proceedings in the meantime," and then all of a sudden he violates his solemn word, goes to the judge, gets an order against the mortgagor and takes possession of the farm, what would you think of him? By a series of subterfuges, and by the use of language for disguising thought, you may endeavour to make the Canadian people believe that you made no promise to them, but in the Speech from the Throne you said that these changes should take place "only" after the fullest examination by this new advisory board. In the most solemn way known to our institutions you made that

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
promise to the people of this country, and in the face of that promise you have violated your pledged word and introduced a measure for reducing the duties without the question having'first been heard by the tariff board at all. You may argue as much as you like, but stripped of everything, the cold facts are there and speak for themselves. Then you go about and endeavour to arouse the passions of the people by making them believe that these rich manufacturers are profiting at their expense, that the people are 'being exploited. You do that in order to make them forget the main issue, in order to make them forget the broken word, the broken faith, the broken promise, and remember only the material benefits. Since when was honour to be sold for dollars?
Let me quote to you, Sir, a word from the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who is good enough to listen to me. This is what he said in the town of Waterloo as reported in his own paper on the 26th of September last:
I voted against the government on the budget of last year, not because of any great injury from the slight reductions in tariff (for no industry in Kitchener or Waterloo was injured), but because I did not like the adoption of a policy of haphazard changes.
Those words I commend to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and to this government. I ask the Minister of Finance now, on what considerations, on what investigation, in view of the promise given in the Speech from the Throne, did he arrive at the conclusion he has stated? The great Gladstone-and whatever else may be said this at least has always been true, that the expositions of financial matters by Mr. Gladstone are still treated as models upon which Chancellors of the Exchequer pattern their deliverances-had something to say about public sentiment in a speech he made in 1860. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, in moving the new automobile duties referred to public sentiment, and I desire particularly to direct attention to the exact words he used in that regard, because they are all important. He said:
There is a pronounced sentiment in this country in favour of a reduction dn automobile duties.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So there was.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Assume there was. Is
it a government at all that yields to sentiment? Such a one is not worthy of the name of government. Listen to the words of Mr. Gladstone when delivering his great budget proposals in 1860, when he proposed to reduce the income tax:
Fot that public feeling we have not only respect, but sympathy; while we do not admit that it is our duty, as persons charged with the conduct of
public affairs, to shape our measures according to any feeling or sentiment whatever, until we have examined the practical form which they are to take, and tried it in the best light of our understanding.
I commend that to the Minister of Finance. I saw many thousands, at least two thousand men and women, gather in front of this parliament building. The practical operation of these tariff changes so filled them with fear of the ultimate result upon their lives, in their homes and in their factories, that they journeyed to this city to present to the government their case. This government heard them, gave them fair words, and they departed. Since then we know that a great effort has been made in many sections of this country to induce the government to reconsider its proposals. It has been said that the government does not propose to do so. I recall history again. Mr. Disraeli pointed out to the farmers of England, to the country squires, that Mr. Peel was getting ready to let them down. Now, in the case of agricultural implements in Canada, remember what happened. The government was adamant. Mr. Bradshaw and Mr. Massey pointed out the ruin that confronted them. No change resulted, but finally, not directly but by removal of the sales tax, by making free the materials that enter into the construction of the machines, the government gave them a higher protection than they had heretofore enjoyed, and they are more prosperous by reason of it than they were before. I ask hon. gentlemen to my left who cheered so lustily when the reduction of the duty on automobiles was announced to pause and ask themselves whether or not they will be once more the victims of deception.

Will the hon. gentleman
permit me to ask him a question?

Mr, BENNETT:	My hon. friend the

gested and the opposition had also suggested -as to the effect of the operation of the removal of the tariff on automobiles or its reduction, that hon. members voted in accordance with their views without the information that might be forthcoming. In violation of that promise, and in breach of the plighted word of this country as represented by the government, the reduction has been made without an investigation. I say further that in private life no man would for a moment tolerate such conduct.
Yesterday I was in New York and picking up one of the newspapers there I read that a great statesman of that country was endeavouring to define national honour. He said that national honour consisted in having the same regard for the obligations of the nation that you have in private life as man to man. I ask:	Is there a man in this
House who, having given a promise such as that contained in the Speech from the Throne, would dare break that solemn promise and call himself a gentleman of honour? Is a pledge given by this government to stand on no higher ground that a scrap of paper or the treaty of Belgium? Let us look this thing fairly in the eye. Is there one standard of honour for individuals and another standard for the nation? The Prime Minister pointed out the other day that he had a duty as leader of this House-not as leader of the government but as leader of the House-representing, as he did, for the moment, the people of Canada. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, would the Minister of Finance in the conduct of his business stoop to sucn conduct as that?

Hon. gentlemen need
not laugh. I put this question to them: If the bank that took a three months' note from you and lent you a thousand dollars on it the next day said. "We are going to sue you because we have changed our minds; we are going to make this a day note instead of a three months' note," what would you think of such conduct? Might is right, that is the theory, the old Prussian theory. When we have a majority a pledge is a scrap of paper. Mi^ht controls the situation; let us do as we please in this matter regardless of our promises. Hon. gentlemen opposite have pledged their solemn word. The pledge is there, they cannot change it. But the word that under our institutions was placed in the mouth of the representative of the sovereign counts for nothing. That representative must now be told that it was all camouflage, that it meant nothing, that it was just a play on words. That is all.

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
I	have here a little information that I am sure would be exceedingly interesting at least to some hon. members. I notice, for instance, that the reduction of the duty upon automobiles is going to be greatly to the benefit of this country, just as was the reduction in the duty on agricultural implements. The argument advanced this afternoon was this: Reduce the duties and you get more people at work. The country is more prosperous and everyone is happy. My hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) said he is against that sort of thing because it is a haphazard way of proceeding. I hope he has not changed his mind. Now let us see what the argument was this afternoon. It was that because in the case of agricultural implements you have alleged benefits, therefore in the case of motor cars you will have similar results. That is the argument, that or nothing. Well, if it means anything at all it means that this House is going to take the sales tax off automobiles and let all the raw material come in free. If it does not mean that it does not mean anything. Now let us know what has
happened. There was a gentleman
II	p.m. named Clifford who once sat in this
House, and he came from Oshawa. He visited Ottawa last week. He went back home and gave an interview to the press and what did he say? This is what he said, and his statements appear between quotation marks:
L. O. Clifford, former M.P. for Ontario who has just returned from Ottawa, where he went for a special conference with lit. Hon. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister, states that he had a long talk with the Premier and has the assurance "that Oshawa will be looked after".
"You can go back to Oshawa, and tell the manufacturers to keep their industries going," Premier King told Clifford, "You may tell the people that their interests will be looked after."

speechtext:
Not for a moment would I suggest him. Judas was a man of great capacity. I desire to point out that since the reduction in the tariff has taken place there have been nine bankruptcies in Oshawa and a prominent lawyer in that city tells me that during the twenty years he has practised there he has not known so much depression. It does not end there. We find from a great American newspaper the net result of this upon the community:
Buick Gets Canadian Order as Result of Reduction in Tariff
The first direct result in the automobile industry from the reduction in the Canadian automobile tariff was reported by the Buick Motor Company, a division of general motors, in the nature of an order for immediate shipment of 50 Buick automobiles to McLaughlin Motor Car Company at Montreal.
H. H. Bassett, president and general manager of the Buick company, in making public the information, stated that this is the first order for a finished car ever received from Canada by the Buick company.
The new cars, Mr. Bassett said, provided the opening to establish a substantial business for American automobile manufacturers in the Dominion of Canada.
In other words for the first time, by reason of this tariff which was not considered by the government in the manner promised, you have completed automobiles imported into the country, and that means just that much less work for Canadians. I do not mean that it is the first time completed automobiles were imported into Canada, but the first time completed automobiles ordered by the manufacturers of cars in Canada were imported into Canada-that is, distinguished from cars in a partly manufactured condition. What does it mean? It means that without regard to promises, with wholly inefficient and inadequate information, without regard to the subsidiary or allied companies, a tariff is placed upon the statute book lower than would have satisfied the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) or lower than the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) was willing to suggest should be imposed, or lower than the
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

Minister of Finance was prepared to suggest. In order to make what would be a popular budget, you have repudiated your promise and put under your foot the Speech from the Throne as though it were a piece of paper. That is my view. I have always advocated that these whole problems should be studied and the duties revised as the facts warranted, and upon that I now stand.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman just stated that fifty Buick automobiles had come into Canada. The duty on these cars would be 27-^ per cent under the reduction. Does he think that duty is too low?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All I know is that any duty which gives an unfair advantage over Canadians to the great people to the south of us is a duty which is not sufficient. By that I am prepared to be judged from one end of the country to the other. Any duty that sacrifices Canadians for foreigners, whoever they are, is not an adequate duty, because it does not safeguard Canadian industry, it simply leaves Canadians to become hewers of wood and drawers of water for our neighbours to the south.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member advocate a prohibitive tariff?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yesterday I observed an advertisement of the Dodge Motors in New York. They have reduced the price of Motors, and they point out how they are able to do it: they state that it was by increasing production, thereby lessening the unit cost. That is the whole story. This country can never become a competitor of our great mass-producing neighbours to the south until we realize that essential fact. My hon. friend asked me if I wanted a prohibitive tariff, and my answer is that I want a tariff that will enable the Canadian manufacturer to go on producing his goods cheaper every year by reason of increased volume of production. For example, we have a repair shop in Calgary, and the overhead is say $6,000 a year or $500 a month. If they repair 500 cars per month it costs $1 a car, but if they repair 1,000 cars it is only 50 cents a car. If we can increase production by preventing competitors from coming in, we will reduce the cost by decreasing the unit cost and in that way we benefit the consumer. There are times when it is more. This party realized that, and they placed in the resolution a provision that if the tariff were taken advantage of for the purpose of exploitation, then the govern-

ment of the day would, by excise or other forms of taxation, protect the consumer from such exploitation by the manufacturer, not only with respect to the effect on a particular industry, but with respect to the effect on others. With respect to that matter I have not the knowledge lo speak with authority, neither have hon. members opposite; but I do know the effect on allied industries, the industry, for instance, that produces the articles that go mto the manufacture. If you go into the pages of history, and if you recall the speech of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Kaiser) and consider the industries that are affected, producing the component parts of the motor industry, you will understand that the tariff is a structure. If you strike out one brick you may impair the whole foundation of the whole wall, and if the wall is impaired what becomes of it? . It is not the tariff on automobiles we are concerned about; it is the effect upon the industrial life of the country and upon the industries involved, the increase of unemployment, the destruction of investment of capital in Canada in any industrial enterprise. Men are already inquiring, what do we get next? I suppose that is the reason the Minister of Finance suggested cottons, in order that those interested in this industry shall keep quiet and not make observations, because they may be struck next. Who is to be struck next? Is it the furniture or the boot and shoe manufacturers? Which is it to be? Is it the artificial silk industry? I put these questions to the House because the destruction of these subsidiary interests in the manner indicated is something no Canadian can look at without having the greatest apprehension as to what the result will be.
My rigffit hon. friend has referred to the income tax reduction, and I shall make just half a dozen observations on that score before I conclude. I say without any hesitation whatever Chat the income tax reductions, of which the government has been making so mudh, are more apparent than real; they are not reductions at all. I do not suppose that any greater bluff was ever worked upon a people. The illustrations given this afternoon by the Prime Minister had reference to incomes earned or incomes treated as though they were earned. Mr. Gladstone once remarked that there were two classes of incomes, one, the lazy income and Che other the income derived from ski'll, enterprise, brains and the salary that one was able to command by reason of ability and acumen. The schedule which the Minister of Finance read to the House a few weeks ago is one in which

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
every dollar of income was put upon a basis of salary or earned income. My right lion, friend will remember that before the amendments were passed at all salaries were taxed to the fullest extent. Now, what has happened? Earned incomes and incomes from investments are all on the same level and the only man who is hit by this tariff is the man who invests his money in a Canadian industrial enterprise. Does the Prime Minister realize just what that signifies? Let us take an illustration. Before the statute was passed, the man who had money invested in American securities had to pay the full amount on his income, just as the salaried man was obliged to do. But if anyone had shares in a Canadian industrial enterprise he was relieved of the normal tax; and this on the old principle of taxation, that the same government should not tax twice the same piece of money. Under the present proposal if a company has $25,000 available for dividends the government takes 9 per cent or $2,250, and that leaves $22,250 for distribution among the shareholders. That money goes into the hands of the shareholders and is taxed on the same basis as the American income or any income that may come from England or Germany. Let us bear that in mind. Now what is the government discriminating against in this connection? It is discriminating against money derived from Canadian industry, so that the $2,250 of taxation which the company I have just suggested by way of illustration has to pay to the government, does not represent the full extent of the tax which is levied on that money inasmuch as every one of the shareholders must pay his private tax. In other words, that $25,000 pays alt the rate of 9 per cent and perhaps 10 pe.r cent more in the hands of the shareholders. Why should the government place such a handicap on Canadian industry? Do hon. gentlemen opposite think that any man would be inclined to invest money in industry in Canada under such circumstances? Yesterday a banker of international reputation said to me, "Mr. Bennett, that is certainly a fine budget which your government has introduced. It will be the means of sending a lot of money to New York for investment." Of course it will, and for three reasons: first, because the return on American investments is larger than on investments made in Canada; secondly, because the investments are more liquid and marketable; and thirdly, because of the assurance and stability due to the tariff policy in force in the United States. What, on the other hand, have we in this country? If a man invests
money in industry here he is taxed to such an extent as to be altogether discouraged from leaving his investment in that industry or adding to it. First of all the government taxes the corporation 9 per cent. Now it is true that in the United States the tax is 13 per cent, but we must remember that the shareholders there are free frjm the normal tax. The company having been once taxed, the government there considers that it would be eminently unfair to tax the individual shareholder a second time on the same money. But we have abandoned that sound principle. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, this is a rich man's budget. Look at the schedule. The man with an income of $250,000 pays nearly fifty thousand dollars less than under the old act; the man with an income of half a million pays over $100,000 less and the man with a very much larger income pays some quarter of a million dollars less than before. But if an individual who has put by some money invests it in a Canadian enterprise yielding 7 per cent he will pay full tax on that $70 income from the thousand dollars of his investment, as he will not be free from the normal tax. The budget is a discrimination against incomes earned from Canadian securities. I could give the names of men and women to-day who have been realizing on Canadian securities and who are now withdrawing their investments and sending their money to the United States, to Great Britain and to France. To-day there is a steady stream of money going to the brokers of Wall street from Canada. It is estimated that as large a sum as $75,000,000 of Canadian money has been invested in government securities of Chile, Argentine, Italy and other countries. This, Mr. Speaker, is not a simple matter. It is one that strikes at the foundation of our whole industrial development, for if capital is to be twice taxed we shall find that people will refuse to invest in Canadian enterprises. I say, therefore, that instead of being a prosperity budget this budget is calculated to turn Class against class. The government will go to the country and say, "Look at what we have done for the poor mam." Well, I know of poor men who have saved money which they have invested in industry, and those men will suffer in consequence of this budget. During the last few years there has been considerable thrift in Canada and men have invested in industrial enterprises, drawing 6 or 7 per cent on preferred Shares. Now their income will no longer be free from the normal tax, and inevitably they will withdraw that money and invest it in the United States
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

'Where they will enjoy the protection of a stable tariff and other advantages to which I have referred.
There is one other matter which I desire
to mention and which arises out of the observations made with respect to the motion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) regarding the tariff board and the question of protection. It was said by the leader of the government that my right hon. leader did not introduce his resolution into this House although he might have done so at any time before the budget iwas brought down. Let me read from the speech of the leader of the opposition:
It is a matter of regret to me, Hr. Speaker, that I am compelled to move this resolution, which has stood upon the order paper since the opening of the session, in -the form of an amendment instead of as a substantive motion. On private members' days, which, under the rules, were alone open to me for this purpose, the order never was reached except at so late an hour of night as to render it impracticable to have it moved and discussed, and the government saw fit to decline to give any special preference to the motion or to fix a day for its discussion as a substantive motion. That it now becomes an amendment to supply and on that account is open to the government to be accepted as a motion of want of confidence, is no choice of mine; it is the only alternative left. I avail myself of that alternative and shall present the reasons why I think the motion should be adopted, why at all events, if it cannot appeal to this House, it should appeal to the people of Canada.

CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, undoubtedly it is cruel to tax the attention of the House at this hour of the night and after this protracted debate. I would certainly much prefer to avoid adding any observations; but in justice to the electors who have sent me here and to a certain category of people in the province of Quebec and elsewhere, whose views I think I fairly represent, I have a few things to say with regai-d to the budget which do not entirely coincide with the views expressed on either side of the House. I will endeavour to confine myself to those.
On the trade returns presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and so eloquently dwelt upon this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), I need not insist. These figures are satisfactory in them-
The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

selves; 'but, on the other hand, the experience of the world and economic evolutions have demonstrated that an increase in trade is not always and under all circumstances an indication of standing prosperity. Increase in trade, either in imports or exports, may mean much or little, or very different things. Increases in imports may mean a decrease in home production or an increase in purchasing power. Increases in exports may indicate a decrease of purchasing power, a decrease in home consumption, or an increase in the foreign debt which is met by merchandise instead of by money. A favourable balance of trade has been many times discussed from various viewpoints. I will not indulge in any theorising on the matter, but I think I express the view of those people who are not particularly interested in the success of one party or the other by saying that the trade situation of the country is fairly satisfactory. It offers an indication of a safe recuperation from the crisis through which we, with the rest of the world, passed during and after the war. It certainly does not warrant the wailings of the Conservative party, expressed previous to the election, during the electoral campaign and since. On the other hand it cannot, be ignored that there is still uneasiness in the country and a disquietude in many spheres of our economic life. The emigration of our population to the United States is still going on, not to the same degree as in years past, but sufficiently to engage the attention of the government and of all people having the welfare of Canada at heart.
As to the primary cause of that situation, to confine it to a fiscal policy which, after all, has been practically the same for the last fifty years is, to my mind, disregarding the real facts of the case. The deeper and more permanent cause of that uneasiness, of that disquietude and emigration to the United States is to be found in our war follies, and this cannot be too much insisted upon in order that future generations may learn by the past. We should be thankful to the Prime Minister for having put his finger this afternoon on that element of the situation. What has been the main cause of the depopulation of our rural districts and the concentration of our people in the large industrial centres, and the volume of unemployment, at times larger and at times smaller, but always a problem since the war? It lays in the war itself, or rather in the exaggerated part we took in it. The enlistment of soldiers took away most of the able-bodied men from the farm and from industry in order to make them destroyers of life, destroyers of wealth and destroyers of economic balance,

instead of keeping them in this country to work for our future generations. Whether we did right or wrong I am not discussing at the moment, but I think we should acknowledge this fact. A further cause of the rural exodus was the building up of those temporary war industries which offered abnormal wages to young people who had no particular propensities for trade or for industry. It brought them to the cities, young women as well as young men, disgusted them with rural life; so that when the war was over and these industries closed, they did not go back to the land. They impoverished the rural part of Canada and kept up the volume of unemployment in the cities to an abnormal degree.
With regard to the balance of wealth, the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan) once quite rightly said on a public platform in Montreal, that while, on the whole, the war had not impoverished Canada, it had displaced wealth. Anything that tends to disturb the economic balance of a country does not make for the good of that particular country. You may have the same amount of money in the country, either deposited in banks, invested in industry, or employed in various ways, but if the apportionment of that amount, represented either by liquid money or by values invested in farming or industry, is not fairly balanced among the masses of the people, you have a poorer country than if you had less money better apportioned. That has been another result of the war.
Then there was created a derangement in the industrial life of Canada, I think it was the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) who mentioned the other day a certain industry which, before the war, made carriage wheels. During the war it was transformed into a munition factory, and, following the war, turned into something else. What does that mean? Does it mean the putting of capital into an industry for the purpose of developing that industry normally? No; on the contrary, it means useless expenditure; it disturbs the industry, its machinery, its labour, and creates uneasiness.
Then, during the war fever and the period of folly which followed, our people fell into habits of extravagance, in the domestic life, in industrial pursuits, in trade enterprises and in the works and expenditures carried on by public bodies, manifesting itself to-day in the abnormal taxation. That is not only on account of the direct expenditures of the war but also results from the indirect expenditure grafted, so to speak, upon the war debt and inflated by the war spirit. It means an increase in the cost of living, an increase in

The Budget

Mr. Bourhssa
the burdens, public and private, of the mass of the people, and therefore it means difficulty, uneasiness and emigration.
The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has spoken of the 500,000 people who have gone to the United States from Canada, and he attributed that exodus to the fiscal policy of this government. He said the only way to call back those people was to confirm a policy of protection. Is protection really the remedy to all our evils? How can it be applied, and to what degree should it be applied? Let us -for a moment consider -protection, first as a means of fostering industrial activity, and then as a mode of taxation.
I was somewhat amused, and felt somewhat like Rip Van Winkle in listening to this long, debate on the respective merits of free trade and protection. It carried me back to -my boyhood1 days. When I first entered political life, I was sent as a delegate from my present constituency to the great Liberal convention held in Ottawa in 1893. The byword of the Liberal party then was that there should be no rest till the last vestige of protection had been destroyed; on that cry the elections of 1896 were carried and won; but, as was explained afterwards, while the rank and file of the Liberals crusaded against protection, the leaders made arrangements with the parties interested in protection, so that there was not much change.
Since then the fiscal policy of Canada has been about the same. In spite of the loud declamations in favour of protection, on the one hand, and the denunciations of protection, on the other, practically we have had the sarnie fiscal policy in this country for the last fifty years. Now, is that policy good or bad? I am beginning to feel somewhat disquieted and, I must say, a little disgusted at hearing always quoted the example of England, on the one hand, as proof that we should adopt free trade, and that of the United States on the other, as evidence that we should go in for a stiff protection. Canada is not England nor is it the United States. For the short time of my life in which I believed in the creed of free trade, even then I had already the habit of trying to understand what I said, which brought me many difficulties in my political life. So I began to study the question. I read Cobdem, Adam Smith, Frederic Bastiat, Moli-nari, and other authorities, and I became convinced that free trade was a great theory. But then, I also had another habit, which I have cultivated, of looking to the applications of theory; and to my great surprise I found out that -free trade.-or rather the policy of free importations, because free trade never
existed-produced, in England, economically and socially, the same results which high protection produced in the United States: concentration of wealth, depopulation of -the rural districts, industrialization of the country, to the same extent, and perhaps more so, in free trade England than in protectionist United States. Why? I think the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Hatfield) told us yesterday: because the geographical, economic and industrial conditions of the two countries were so different that two different policies could produce the same results.
Canada cannot and never will be the shipping country which England is, and therefore can never expect from the exchange of her merchandise on all the seas the same results which a free importing country like England has obtained, thanks to her geographical position and to her search for foreign markets in all neutral lands and in almost all semi-civilized countries on the face of -the earth. Canada, on the other hand, cannot expect to be as self-sufficient a country as the United States. The climate is against us; the geographical configuration of the country is against us. There will always be more difficulty in creating a well balanced internal trade in Canada. There will always be greater difficulty in balancing the agricultural needs of the central provinces and the industrial development of the east. Instead of trying to hypnotize ourselves with the results of the policy obtained in England, under conditions which cannot exist here, or with the 'results obtained in the United States, under conditions which are different from ours, why not at last take an inventory of the real conditions of our country and think and act as Canadians instead of being mere copiers of England or the United States?
Especially am I always surprised at finding that the Conservative party, which boasts so much of its loyalty to -all British institutions and precedents. British -example and British traditions, should have become so thoroughly imbued with the Yankee spirit in matters of trade and economics. I am not prepared to say, as the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) said a short time ago, that the policy of protection necessarily makes for war and hatred between nations. There again -history would prove that free trade England has looked for more wars, has waged more wars, and provoked more wars, on account of her free trade policy, than the United States have ; and the United States -were more often at war before they became protectionist than they
The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

have been since they adopted the high tariff policy; but that, I think, proves nothing one way or the other.
Let us take protection as it has worked in Canada, for the last fifty years, and as applied by the protectionist party. Has it produced all the results which we are told it *would produce if applied now? And should" it be on a higher scale of duties than was established by the Conservative government previously? We have heard nothing as to that, except the famous " brick for brick " declaration. But as protection has been applied under the Conservative regime, by the party which invented protection as a gospel and a policy, what has it produced? It has undoubtedly created and developed some large industries. But it has also contributed to crush a great many small and local industries. Perhaps as the hon. member for Wellington once said, I lack the practical spirit. But, to my mind, not being interested in any industry whatever, I consider that a greater wealth and a more enduring prosperity would result in this country by the spreading and maintenance of small local and domestic industries, in every province of Canada, than by the concentration of large industries in a few cities of Ontario and Quebec. In that respect I ,am not only expressing the view of an unpractical French-Quebecker, but it is one of the main arguments made last year in the province of Nova Scotia by one of the leaders of the Conservative party, by a colleague, for a time, I think, of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), certainly of the hon. member for Calgary and of the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen)-an argument made by the Hon. Mr. McCurdy, who pointed out that the National Policy, so-called, and as applied under both Conservative and Liberal governments, has destroyed all industries in Nova Scotia. I need not read the extract, I gave it during the debate on the Address. In Ontario and even in Quebec, the same result has obtained, to a lesser degree, but sufficient to drive the rural population from the farming districts to the urban centres. More so in Ontario than in Quebec, because the industries in Ontario are more even dispersed in various centres of medium size, whilst in Quebec, up to a few years ago, the large industries were practically all centred in Montreal, Quebec and a few other towns. But since a new impetus has been given to industry in the province of Quebec the same process is taking place. Four or five years ago, I was passing through that magnificent region lying north and south of lake St. Peter, those splendid rural districts which have been counted as the most

fertile producing parts of Quebec at least, if not of Ontario as well. Well, the population of these districts has diminished largely in the last ten or twenty years . Some of the people have gone to industrial centres such as Three Rivers, Shawinigan Falls and Grand'Mere. Many others-seeing their sons leave the farm and go to work as labourers in the city, seeing also their daughters follow them to become operatives in factories or to-adopt some other occupation-have abandoned the farm because they no longer had the family labour at hand to cultivate it. This has been one of the main causes of the migration of our rural populations to the United States. Thus the over-industrialization of Ontario and Quebec had begun this process of unrooting our rural population long before the war. The war simply gave a new impetus to the process. It also began to have this effect:	Producing wealth,
not properly balanced, impoverishing gradually the villages and the rural districts and enriching the industrial centres, it created in our cities, as in every other industrialized country, this double curse of modern times: plutocracy and pauperism. In spite of all statistics-large deposits in banks, stock exchange reports, et cetera, this does not mean wealth, still less prosperity and happiness.
But there is something more. Most of the industries in this country, created under the protective system, organized themselves without any state supervision, without any legal control as the real amount of capital invested therein, and the amount of water added to the real amount of capital. What is the result? To-day the purchasing people of this country are paying for the commodities they consume, for the goods they use, not only a fair remuneration upon the real amount of capital invested in the making of those goods; but are making returns to the financial sharks upon the amount of watered stock, of valueless paper, all called "capital." I do not believe in that. If you take these two things together, there is sufficient explanation to be found of the fact that the industrialization of this country has not benefited the whole of the Dominion, and there need be no surprise that some of our provinces should entertain a feeling of distrust, almost akin to hatred, against other provinces which they hold responsible for the state in which they find themselves.
But somethng more, and from a national point of view something of a more disquieting nature has occurred, especially since the war. I stood for protection, reasonable protection, for many years, because I thought it

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
was one of the obstacles to the penetration of our country by American influences. But since the war, and largely on account of our war follies, our fiscal and economic regime is now tending to make Canada a field for the investment of American capital. Some people rejoice in that. I do not. I think there is more danger to the national independence of Canada in the purchasing of our w&iterpowers, and of our sources of wealth, either in the forest or an the mine, by American capital than there is from the fact that some of our industries suffer from the competition caused by American merchandise entering this country. It is all very well to say that American capitalists and industrialists are coming to this country because they find 'conditions here suitable to their purpose-that they would not advocate any sudh thing as political or economic union with the United States. So long as the social and economic conditions of Canada were sulch that it was to the advantage of the American investor to maintain this state of things, very well. But now that we have higher taxation in Canada than in the United States-because we were more foolish during the war than the Americans were, because we spent more money, because we ruined more people, because we uprooted more of our young population from the soil for war purposes than the Americans did-the economic and social Conditions in this country are getting to be such that it is becoming more advantageous, from a purely economic point of view, to invest and to live in the United States than in Canada. When the American investor finds out that his investment in Canada, that the development of his trade in Canada,- shut off from the United! States by the American tariff,-is less profitable to him than his investment in the country to the south, that he is running just as much risk, if not more, and reaping less profit than he would in the1 United States, it will not take a lifetime before he finds means-perhaps with the help of a portion of the Canadian press and a good many of our ultra patriots-to start a movemept that may take the form of independence, to begin with, but will have for its object economic union at first and afterwards political union with the United States.
There is more to be feared than the penetration by American capital. American capital does not ,come into Canada as English capital used to come, merely as an investment. Those great industries which are put up and developed by American capital, are also managed by American citizens with all their genius, their spirit of enterprise, their courage and
their energy,-no doubt a splendid thing from a purely material and economic point of view, and I am second to none in rendering homage to the genius and energy of the American people and their great cap-12 m. tains of industry. But they also bring with them, and naturally, without any effort or any propaganda, spread around them the spirit of Americanism. I have already noticed in the province of Quebec, where industries have been established by Americans and are managed by Americans, a new social spirit among the people working for them and living near them. With the penetration of capital, is coming the penetration of habits of work, the penetration of social habits. Over and above that, there is the penetration of the so called American literature, which the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) mentioned the other day, in the form of American magazines, Sunday papers, and so forth; and again we bad ithe manifestation of that characteristic Yankee tendency which prevails on that side of the House in the suggestion !by him of a remedy in the shape of "protection" by way of a customs duty. He says that it would not prevent a better class of American publications from coming in, because people would gladly pay the duty, but that it would shut off the worst class. I believe the contrary. People who are looking for the worst class of American publications will gladly pay ten or fifteen cents more to have them and read them; but the seriously inclined people will perhaps hesitate before paying thirty-five or fifty cents for the serious American review. Here again I suggest that the remedy is not simply the imposition of a duty. The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) said. "Do not count honour by dollars." I say do not combat foreign influences by the mere imposition of a duty. If you want to counteract the influence of American publications in this country, you must develop in all spheres of life the spirit of Canadian nationalism. It is not by making the people more British that you will prevent them becoming more American but it is by making them more Canadian. The hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) had the courtesy of saying that the province of Quebec was better preserved from that penetration. Quite true. But why? The province of Quebec is better preserved on account of its language first; but a large and increasing number of our people read and learn the English language thoroughly. The language barrier itself would not be sufficient. Unfortunately, too large a proportion of that
The Budget

Mr. Bourassa

influx of American literature comes into the province of Quebec and penetrates Canadian homes; but it has less effect, not only because of the language but because of the religious spirit and social tradition inherited by centuries of attachment to the soil of Canada. It is because we are more thoroughly and exclusively Canadian. I am surprised that people who are so prone to denounce the penetration of American influences do not realize that the greatest moral strength we can use to counteract that penetration is by inducing as many French Canadians as we can to settle and live in the English speaking provinces of Canada, not as foreigners, but as Canadians, to help to stamp in those provinces that type of social life that has made the province of Quebec, and which still maintains in that province, the only real obstacle to Americanism which remains in Canada.
It has been stated several times that Quebec i3 protectionist, and that Quebec, had it not been for the conscription or other war issues, would have voted protectionist. I am surprised at the creation and the maintenance of tha-t legend. I take it for granted that many of those who express that view speak in good faith. Undoubtedly it is due to the fact that some newspapers in Quebec, with a large circulation, controlled by men of strong influence, consider themselves the whole of Canada, of the empire and perhaps of the world. Being protectionist they think and assert that the whole province must be protectionist. On this matter I will take the testimony of a good friend of our province, one who knows it well, who has lived in it for some years, who i3 a pronounced protectionist and an avowed Conservative. I refer to my excellent friend the member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Oahan). A year ago last fall, there was a byj election in the city of Montreal in the St. Antoine division, decidedly one of the most Conservative and protectionist ridings of tbu whole province. The election was fought purely and simply, as this debate has been, on what these gentlemen call the principle of protection, and the protectionist candidate was defeated, upon which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George wrote a very interesting letter; I thought it was the most complete expression of opinion on the political situation at large, and especially in Quebec. It appeared in the Montreal Gazette on December 10, 1924, and in it Mr. Cahan stated:
I was especially impressed during the last election contest in St. Antoine division iby the number of former supporters of a protective tariff who expressed reluctance to vote for Mr. Birks. They recognized the personal moral worth and the commercial and industrial standing of the Conservative candidate; but they were not quite satisfied with that kind of pro-

tectron which Mr. Meighen seemed to advocate.
More or less casual conversations with my fe31ow-electors at (the clu/bs and on the street have clearly convinced me that the electors have now begun to discriminate between the general policy of protection and the incidence of the existing customs tariff; between the existing high customs duties which unduly favoured certain industries, and the existing low customs duties which tend to drive other industries out of existence. When invited to vote for a protective policy, (they instinctively enquired: "Protection to which industry, and to whom?"
In those conversations several industries were frequently referred to which, in the course of years, by corporate consolidations effected under the law or by commercial agreements formed within the law, had become infant prodigies and practical monopolies, which, by taking full advantage of the existing tariff, were thereby enabled to deal harshly with the consumers.
It is evident that the high cost of living, the imposition of income taxes and the existing precarious conditions of employment, have led thousands of voters to discriminate between -that kind of protection which would enable Canadian industries to withstand foreign competition and to create local employment, and that other kind of protection which would continue to enable a monopoly to oppress the local consumers.
I think I may take this as the full and candid expression of the reasoned' opinion pf the protectionist Conservatives of the province of Quebec generally. Now when you come to the mass of the rural population, to consider that they are protectionist by tradition or habit is to ignore the whole history of the province. The province of Quebec has never responded to an appeal for high protection but has voted against ail such appeals.

speechtext: Is the hon. member ia favour of protection as a principle?

speechtext: I do not see any principle in protection.
