speechtext: Then what is -the principle he stands for in regard to the tariff?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will wait, I will endeavour to express as shortly as possible what I think is the view of the great mass of the people of the province of Quebec on this issue: of the thinking man by reasoning, and of the mass by instinct and tradition. We do not make a religion either of free trade or protection-at least I do not. As I toid my hon. friend, for a couple of years I believed in free trade almost as much as in my creed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Free trade as it is practised in England?

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When I was a greenhorn I believed in free trade as it is practised there, but as I got to know something I believed in nothing. I think the best policy for this country is a policy suited to our needs and conditions, and for that reason I stand for no principle in tariff matters and for no stability, so far as duties are 'concerned.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No principle?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No; it is purely a matter of business, which must be governed by the circumstances of time and 'locality and by geographical and climatic considerations. We stand in Quebec-at least, I do, and I think that in expressing my personal views I am voicing the opinions of a large number of people in that province-we stand, I say, for a reasonable measure of protection. We stand for home industries, by which term we mean industries that use our native products, mineral or animal.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will let me develop my point he will see better whether there is any necessity for him to ask his question. I am at one with gentlemen opposite in advocating a policy, not of embargo but of encouragement, aimed at inducing capitalists or industrialists who have money invested in our forests and mines to develop their industry, and so far as conditions will permit, to manufacture their products up to the finished state in this country. I believe in turning all Canadian wood into *Canadian paper, so far as we can possibly do so, rather than allowing our wood to go to the United States to enrich American manufacturers. I believe in converting Canadian minerals, nickel, asbestos, and so forth, into finished commodities, rather than allowing them to go to the United States to enhance United States capital; I prefer to have them developed in Canada and so afford employment to Canadian labour. I believe, again, in protecting the beet sugar industry, and in that respect I entirely agree with the hon. member for East Lambton' (Mr. Armstrong). But I certainly do not believe in a tariff policy which has succeeded in creating a sugar monopoly in the hands of a few men in Montreal and elsewhere in Canada and enabling them, by means of sugar duties, not only to receive incomes from the capital, they have invested in Canada but also to maintain the sugar plantations which they have purchased in Cuba and in the West Indies. In short, if "by encouragement to local industry we mean, as in this instance, protection for beet sugar .growing I am in favour of a policy that will 14011-224
assist our producers. But let that policy be one such as is in force in Germany, Belgium, and France. Let us encourage the growers of beets in this country rather than the producers of cane in Cuba and the West Indies, because all the genius of all the Conservative leaders and partisans will never make cane growing possible in this country. Likewise, I am opposed to protection on cotton in the degree and in the manner in which it has been afforded in Canada during the past forty years, forcing the masses of the people to pay from 25 to 50 per cent more for all their cotton goods than they would have had to pay for cottons produced either in England or in the United States. I am opposed to such protection for the reason that the soil of Canada will never produce raw cotton; and, for another reason, that the industry, in Quebec at least, has been over-capitalized. Its stock has been watered to the limit, so that every time we buy a yard of cotton in any form, we are making remunerative not only the legitimate capital invested in the industry, but the watered stock that has been added to it. For that kind of protection I have never stood and I never will stand. On the other hand, I am in favour of protection on woollens, because, in my opinion, if properly applied, such protection should be an encouragement, both to the makers of woollen goods and to the farmers who raise sheep and sell their wool. I was very much interested in the proceedings at a meeting in Toronto last-fall of an association of people interested in the woollen industry. I was struck not only by statements made by manufacturers but by the views expressed by farmers. At that meeting, Mr. Dryden, of Maple Shade farm, of Brooklin, Ontario, director of the Canadian Co-operative Wool Growers' Association, spoke as follows:
We can grow successfully in Canada every type of sheep, including merino. Sheep breeding in Canada is economically sound, because our flocks are not subjected to droughts which occur in other sheep breeding countries or suffer from the diseases which have to 'be faced by the sheep breeder in Great Britain. Yet in the small area of Great Britain they maintain 24,000,000 sheep, while in Canada we maintain only 2,500,000, while we now only grow same 15,000,000 pounds of wool. There are no climatic or physical reasons why we should not grow 50,000,000 pounds of the 70,000,000 pounds of wool consumed annually by the people of Canada. Sheep fit into the business of mixed farming as no other farm animal does and in any opinion the raising of sheep in this country is directly connected with successful farming. There should be a flock of sheep on each Canadian farm.
I entirely agree with that. Protection, so far as the woollen industry is concerned, should be applied in such a manner as to



The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
force the manufacturers to buy their raw material from [DOT]local producers. They should use wool grown in Canada and should not be enabled to import their wool from foreign countries, afterwards making the Canadian people pay unreasonable prices to swell their capital.
iWith regard to boots and shoes, the same reasoning holds good. This is an industry which to a very large extent has been implanted in Quebec. I do not want to jplead the case against them, but I desire to give to the House the testimony of one of the best informed men in that industry, the manager of one of the most successful boot and shoe factories in the province of Quebec. A few years before the close of the war he said to me: "After this war is over the boot and shoe industry will pass through the greatest crisis in its history." I asked him why he thought so, and he said that he was of this opinion because, carried away by the allurements of war profits, the operators of most factories were changing their equipment. They were leasing-they could not purchase them- from the American Shoe Machinery Company, machines specially adapted to the making of army boots. They were obliged to pay royalties on these machines and were engaging large numbers of new labourers, educating them in the use of this special machinery which would be absolutely of no use after the war. After the war, he said, the manufacturers would find their factories overequipped, while they will still be compelled to pay royalties to the American company. They will also have on their hands labour utterly unsuited to the trade on a peace basis. This is exactly what happened.
So far as woollens and boots and shoes are concerned, I think I may safely say that the industries to-day are suffering, not because the average duty is too low, but exclusively by reason of the application of the British preference and because of a lack of expert appraisal at the customs. There, again, I have received all my information at firsthand. Under the British preference as applied during the past twenty-five years by both Conservative and Liberal governments, not only do British goods enter into keen competition with the products of these two industries in Canada, but goods manufactured in France, Belgium and Germany, under depreciated currencies, are foisted upon the Canadian market in competition with our manufacturers. These goods are 90 per cent manufactured in these foreign countries; and after receiving a small finishing touch in 
England they are stamped as British and are imported into Canada in competition with Canadian labour, and, for that matter, with British labour as well. In other words, under that famous British preference policy, we are protecting not only British capital and British labour at our own expense, but French, Belgian and German labour and capital. The only profiteer within the British Empire is the British trader who, since the development of social and economic difficulties in England, finds it more profitable to have his goods made in foreign countries and shipped to Canada under the so-called British preference policy.

speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend. I think during the war the boot and shoe makers prepared what happened to them afterwards by the extravagant prices they then asked for their product.. On the other hand, will the hon. gentleman go the length of saying that we should handicap industries established in Canada-always with the reservation that they be honestly capitalized and properly managed,-in favour of foreign articles made under conditions that cannot last, their price being depreciated by reason of abnormal conditions?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend's address, 'but I should like to know how he would keep down domestic prices unless by some outside competition?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh yes, I want competition, but I want fair competition. I want, for example, absolute competition with regard to all those industries that go on the foreign market to purchase their raw material and come and manufacture it here. But when you have an industry which is a help not only to the capitalist, not only to the labourer, but also to the farmer, I say this is a national industry for which all classes of people should be prepared to make some sacrifice-not an undue sacrifice-just as I consider we should be prepared to make some sacrifice to help the western farmer to get his product more rapidly and more cheaply to the grain markets of the world. Likewise the western farmer Should be prepared to pay 25 or 50 cents more for a pair of boots-in order to keep up an industry which is national in its character and which makes use

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
of goods produced in Canada and which will help their fellow farmers in the eastern provinces.
The disposition taken by the government with regard to the application of the British preference is a good one, and so far as it will apply only to goods coming through Canadian ports I could not be against what I advocated in this House some twenty-four years ago. But I think we should go further. In that respect I think we should imitate the example of the Australians and see that at least 80 to 85 per cent of these so-called British-made goods are really British-made, and that no foreign goods should be imported as so-called British-made goods.
Having said so much with regard to protection as an economic policy what about it as a mode of taxation? In this respect I must say that I am perhaps worse than I was twenty-five years ago! As a means of raising revenue I think it is absolutely indefensible. I believe much less in a so-called "tariff for revenue" policy than in a frank and open protective policy. If it is protective, then it is no revenue producer. If it produces revenue, then it is no protection, because when you get revenue you must import goods, and therefore you must eliminate the protective element. Then I am opposed to protection as a mode of taxation because it is essentially directed against the family, and because it is a mode of taxation which the taxpayer realizes the least. Hundreds of thousands of excellent people in this country would vote against any government which would tax them $25 a year, but who, without knowing it, ungrudgingly pay $200 indirectly, either to the government by way of customs duties added to the price of the goods they purchase, or by the higher price they pay for the goods of the protected manufacturer. I believe in the saying of John Morley, that the tax-gatherer is a great school master; but in order that the lesson taught to the taxpayer is not lost, he must realize the amount of money he pays to the state and for what purpose. Therefore I entirely agree with some of those gentlemen on the other side who have said they would much prefer increasing direct taxation and diminishing indirect taxation.
As regards direct taxation, this budget is in many respects an improvement. I will not refer to the Victory bonds exempt from taxation. That was a great mistake and an injustice to the people of Canada. Perhaps there might have been some excuse at the time those bonds were issued), but I consider that instead of decreasing the taxation the 1401}-2241
people have to pay in order to reduce our war debt, we should increase it. It is unjust to our children to lay upon their shoulders the whole burden accumulated by our follies during four years of war. Let those people who are responsible for the war, for the enlistment of men, for conscription, for war expenditure far beyond the normal means of this country, far beyond the moral or political obligations of this country, in order to keep up that military display which has been so scathingly described by Sir Andrew Mac-phail, let those people-.all of us, since we are all responsible,-let our generation pay for that folly, and at the same time let us have the courage and the disinterestedness to say to those who follow us: Do not repeat our folly. I say again, it is unjust to diminish war taxation as long as the war generation lives. I agree entirely with the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworthl that what strict social justice would have demanded would have been a capital levy immediately after the war, so as to reach the immoral, the abnormal and abominable profits made during the war, out of the blood and the blinded patriotism of this country, by warmongers who khouted "King and Country" while they were pocketing money at the expense of our people. I remember the excellent saying of Sir Thomas White, on one occasion in Montreal, that it was a crime for any Canadian to get rich during the war. Well, if that was the case, why has no government had the courage to apply proper punishment to that crime by levying a sufficient amount on those immoral profits so as to lift the burdens of the war from the shoulders of those who were not responsible for it?
With regard to other taxation, the receipt tax perhaps might have remained; but it was very much evaded and, as has been well said, was an annoyance rather than a source of revenue. I would maintain the tax on cheques and, indeed, increase it. I received the other day from a man in business a statement showing how this tax applied. He had a list of cheques he had either paid or received, I am not sure which, during a period of two or three months. By the accumulation of small cheques he had paid quite a sum of money, but on one single cheque of some $15,000 or $20,000 he had paid only $1. I think the limit of $1 on cheques is too low, and should be increased. The reduction in postage does not appeal to me; it was not a very heavy burden on the average' ratepayer and could have remained for a few years longer. I admit it is not popular to say so, but we must have the
352S

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
courage to teach our people that we must pay our debts more quickly than we have been doing. \\ 'e must therefore preserve, I think, all the means of taxation and revenue which are not too burdensome on the average man.
With regard to the sales tax, there are certainly some corrections still to be made. I sent the Minister of Customs (Mr, Boivin) a statement the other day, showing the absurdity of the application of that tax in certain cases. A small lumber dealer with a small shop classed as a factory is obliged to obtain a license. Last year he sold to the farmers around him $2,300 worth of goods, out of which he and his family lived. He employs his son and one workman, yet he was taxed $110 on this $2200 of gross receipts, which included the cost of his material. That is nonsense. The sales tax on small industries of that nature which are local, belonging to the small social economic life of the village or parish, should be abolished.
It is different with the tax on profits. 1 read in the press that a delegation from Montreal came here requesting the government to abolish the tax on the profits of so-called public utilities. They made a very eloquent plea because of the difference in treatment accorded the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario and these so-called public utilities in Quebec. Let us understand each other. The public utilities in Quebec at present are, or in the very near future will be, one single monopoly composed of various corporations interlocked with each other in the hands of two or three men, one of whom is Sir Herbert Holt. Let us examine the position of that so-called public utility, and its service to the public. I am not taking my facts from a socialist organ, but from the Montreal Gazette of February 19, 1924, in which is reproduced an article appearing in the Financial Post. That shows how the genius of Sir Herbert Holt has developed this industry. I am not going to- read the article at length, but some parts of it are very interesting. It explains that Sir Herbert Holt began by taking the old Montreal Gas Company and the Royal Electric Company and [DOT]developing them with such ability, that at present the shareholders of the Montreal Light Heat and Power Consolidated, who had shares of $100 in these companies now hold, without having disbursed one cent of money, 7i shares of the new concern, equivalent, according to current market quotations, to $1,100. But, they say, all along the company has shown great consideration for the public, and the present dividend is limited	to	7 per cent.	But 7 per

cent, on a capital multiplied seven and a half times, means 52i per cent; so that, at the present time, the ratepayers of the city of Montreal, of the island of Mbntreal, and before long practically one-half the province of Quebec, will be remunerating the shareholders of these companies to the extent of 52| per cent, which perhaps will be multiplied by four before very long. That has come about through the high protective policy of the Taschereau government which has found such praise by hon. gentlemen opposite, and which the Montreal Gazette very properly qualified as "a T ory of a T ory " government. The " protection " afforded to the public utilities of Quebec means that the companies under Sir Herbert Holt have laid their hands on all the water power around the island of Montreal; they have prevented so far the development of the Long Sault by rival companies, all for the benefit of the people, of course! Now they come and ask, in the name of the people, to be exempted from taxes on profits. I hope this government will now be sufficiently informed of the situation to resist that demand.
With regard to the income tax, I approve almost unreservedly of the changes which have been made. The increased margin of exemption was called for; the government have eradicated the absurd and unjust discrimination between married people under the laws of the English speaking provinces and those under the laws of Quebec, which discrimination has existed ever since the establishment of the tax. It took nine years to get this reform, and I congratulate the government on having made the change. Respecting the exemption on children I repeat what I said at the beginning of the session, namely, that the exemption should be extended to the age of twenty-one years. \\ e pretend that we want to encourage higher education, and that we want to give inducements to all fathers of families to give as complete an education as possible to their children. I do not know how it goes in the English speaking provinces, but in the backward province of Quebec, with its antiquated system of education, we want our children to learn our own language and all that it carries with it, and we desire them also to learn the language of our fellow citizens of English origin. There we desire to carry on the education of our children as long as we possibly can, and I think this government should have lengthened the exemption to twenty-one years of age, as an inducement to fathers of families to continue the education of their children. It will certainly come in time; it

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
took three years to get the first exemption, and it has been increased gradually.
The change which jmts the householder, unmarried but with family charges, on the same footing as married people, is also an excellent one. There are in our province many young men and, I will not say young girls, or old maids, but less-young girls, who carry on the heavy but sacred social duty of looking to the education of young children who have been left orphans, young brothers and sisters. It is proper, it is just, it is a social duty that they should be treated just as fathers and mothers of families are.
A point was made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) which I think was very well taken, and which I uphold entirely, as to the discrimination between the ratepayer who owns his home and the leaseholder under the present system. The owner of a house is not obliged to take into account the yearly value of his property as forming part of his revenue, while the leaseholder is taxed upon his revenue without any deduction as to the amount he pays in rental. The hon. member made a comparison with a farmer, but the comparison can be made the other way. I know people in Montreal who live in houses certainly worth $100,000 or perhaps $200000, representing a yearly value, let us say, of 5 per cent. They do not pay a cent of taxation for the enjoyment of that property, and I think that is not just. I think that there should be deducted from the charges as against income a yearly value of about $600, representing the average rental, which would go in favour of the property owner as well as of the leaseholder, and that the owners of expensive property should pay something on the yearly value of the house they inhabit.
As to the tax on dividends, well, I would
have bad grace to criticise that, because I asked for it; I have been asking for it for many years. It is called a duplication of taxes. I cannot see it that way. But suppose, first, that it is. There are many things upon which we pay taxation several times. Take real estate, for instance, bringing in revenue; we pay the municipal taxes, we pay the school taxes, and we pay the income tax. Why should the stockholder be more favoured than the owner of real estate? It has been said that we must encourage investment in industry, Very well, but I am more concerned with people who invest in homes and cradles than with people who invest in factories. If a company has made profits, after it has paid its taxation and the rest of its profits are distributed among its shareholders, if those shareholders draw an income from the company equivalent to a salary which is earned year after year, why should the man or the woman who enjoys an income of $5,000 or $6,000 from that investment pay less taxation than the man who earns $5,000 or $6,000 from his labour? The employees of these profit-distributing companies are taxed on their salaries; why should not the stockholders be taxed on their dividends? In many cases I am sure the managers or boards of directors of these companies will abject to giving salary increases to their employees on the ground of the taxation they have to pay. Therefore, as the income of the employee is limited because of the taxation levied on the company, why should not the stockholder also be limited in the profits he may draw, by reason of the taxation? I think that is essentially just and equitable.
It is also said that this tax is discriminating against Canadian -companies. I do not read the act that way. Any Canadian who invests in foreign companies is obliged under the present law to declare his income from foreign investments and to pay -according to the same scale of taxation as if he had invested in real estate or in a Canadian Company. Of course, I admit that there is more chance of evasion if you hold stock in a foreign company, but you have that in every country of the world. I was told the other day by someone who knows very well the functioning of the income tax in England that the amount of English capital invested abroad for the purpose of evasion of taxation is enormous. The same thing exists in France, Germany, Belgium, everywhere. You cannot stop it. But the idea of making of the stockholder a privileged ratepayer in -this -country, or rather of -preventing -him being a ratepayer, of not taxing him on his personal income apart- from the taxation levied on the profits of the company, that I have never been able to understand, and I think the government has made a wise readjustment. Of course, proper care should be taken to collect the tax upon income derived from foreign investments and upon debenture coupons. I do not know, but I have been informed by -people in Montreal who have a deep and intimate knowledge of financial operations that a very large amount of money invested in coupon bonds evades taxation-I do not agree with someone who spoke this afternoon against the idea of a stamp tax. If a stamp tax was imposed upon debenture coupons that are -collected through Canadian banks, and the holders of those debentures were -allowed to deduct that revenue from their tax bill in Canada, probably the result would be much more favourable to the Finance minister than it is at -the present time.

The Budget-Mr. Bourassa
With regard to the increase or the decrease, in the income tax, I am rather inclined to agree with my hon. friend from West Calgary that this is no decrease of taxation. It is better than that; it is a readjustment of taxation, and that is what we need. For the reasons that I have given, for reasons of morality, for reasons of social justice, and for reasons of sound business, this is not the time to reduce taxation. But this is the time, and it is always the time to readjust taxation from year to year, in order to maintain a sound economic balance as between country and city, as between farming and industrial life, as between the various portions of Canada. That is what I call a budget nationally thought out, a proper and socially equitable budget, I do not say that it entirely responds to ail requirements, but it is certainly a move in the right direction. It is certainly a budget that tends towards a better balanced application of taxes than we have had in this country since the war, and therefore, with the suggestions that I have made, and which I hope the Minister of Finance will take into account this year, and next year, and in all the years to come, readjusting the taxation from year to year, I propose to vote for this budget and to maintain the policy of this government, rather than to tie myself to the narrow policy of the Conservative party looking to protection, undefined, unbalanced protection, as the sole and only remedy for all the evils of this country. I did not believe in that remedy in years past. I believe still less in it under the present circumstances, and still less when all that great policy of upholding the principle of protection falls down under the four wheels of a motor car.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I address myself to the question before the House, I should like to say that I feel very sorry indeed that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is not with us to-day. I am sure that we would all have been delighted to have had him here and heard him address this House. Because of the circumstances under which he is absent,
I am sure we all hope that he will very soon be in a position to return again to this House.
Before I discuss the features of the budget I want to refer to some remarks uttered by hon. gentlemen during the present debate. The hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken), in discussing the conditions in Canada, placed before the House a few days ago an idea to this effect: That industry in Canada had not been prospering during the last few years. He quoted certain figures and facts from the reports of the twro great Canadian railway companies to show that fMr. Bourassa.]
agricultural products had been moving in greater quantity than had industrial products, and because of that fact he maintained that Canadian industries had been passing through a very serious time. If I may I would read the quotation in question, and it is this:
My argument therefore is that the traffic arising from sources other than the carriage of farm -products was substantially lc6s in 1925 than in the year before so that in consequence we had a greater degree of general business depression last year.
On looking up the reports of these railway companies I found that everything he affirmed was true except the hon. gentleman's conclusion. With the permission of the House I will place certain traffic figures on Hansard, and I will merely refer to them to show the increase or the decrease in the volume of various commodities carried by our railway companies.

Taking the report of the freight movement of the Canadian National railways for the years 1924 and 1925, and considering that agricultural products were supposed to have moved in greater quantity in 1925 than in 1924, I find the hon. member was incorrect in his statement. I will not state the total amounts moved but will merely give the increases and the decreases as they are taken from the report. The decrease in the amount of agricultural products moved in 1925 as compared with the year 1924 was 144,479 tons.

The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
The decrease in animal products carried in 1925 as against 1924 was 12,647 tons. Of products of the mines there was an increase in the amount carried in 1925 over 1924 of 671,006 tons. Of products of the forest there was an increase in 1925 as compared with 1924 of 360,437 tons. Of manufactures and miscellaneous products there was an increase in 1925 over 1924 of 1,626,326 tons. The grand total of increases for 1925 amounted to 2,500,643 tons. In the case of agricultural products the decrease in movement in 1925 amounted to 157,126 tons. The increase in tonnage of products of the forests and mines, and manufactures and miscellaneous, in 1925 amounted to 2,657,769 tons. These figures dispose altogether of the statement which the hon. member made. It proves very conclusively that the Canadian National Railways moved a greater tonnage of manufactured goods than it did of agricultural products in 1925. In view of these facts it is unfortunate that the hon. member should have made the mistake he did.
Now taking the Canadian Pacific annual report for the year ending December 31, 1925 we find the movement of freight set out at page 35 and I quote from it the following figures: The movement of flour in 1925 was decreased to the extent of 906,370 barrels. There was an increase in the volume of grain moved of 31,657,227 bushels or 949,716 tons. There was an increase of 30,787 head in the number of live stock moved. The movement of lumber increased in the same year, that is 1925, by 56,642 thousand feet. In the movement of manufactured articles there was an increase of 502,664 tons. The movement of all other articles increased by 831,765 tons.
May I explain to hon. members who are not conversant with conditions in western Canada -what happened there during the last two or three years. In the year 1923 we had perhaps one of the best crops in the history of the west. Now, when a good crop is assured in western Canada there is a general movement of trade because the people of the west require many necessaries to enable them to handle their crops. In the year 1923 we had a "carry over'' of grain products to the following year and that was included in the tonnage moved in 1924. In 1924 we had a very light crop in western Canada, consequently there was a reduction not only in the quantity of grain but of manufactured products moved. In 1925 we had no "carry over" of grain which the railways move in the spring. That explains why the situation was of that nature which the statistics indicate. I repeat that the hon. gentleman misrepresented the
fact when he stated that manufactured goods had not been moved in an increased volume of tonnage.
The hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Murphy) in his speech referred to the Progressive movement in western Canada. He stated that the Progeessive movement there was declining. He made a further statement with respect to a certain farmers' periodical, namely, the Grain Growers' Guide, which was challenged by another hon. member. The statement of the hon. member for Neepawa was to this effect:
Until the present time the subscription price has been $2 a year, $1 of which went .to .pay for the paper, the other dollar being the membership fee in the Farmers' Local.
And so on. Now, Sir, I have been a subscriber to the Grain Growers' Guide from the year it was first printed, and I have never known my dues to the Farmers' local to be paid by the Grain Growers' Guide. I know from personal experience that statement is absolutely incorrect, and it is no indication of the hon. gentleman's intelligence to have made such an assertion.
Now, I wish to say a few words with regard to the budget. In the first place I think the budget will be accepted generally by the people of this country. I sat in this House during the last parliament and in my opinion this is the best budget that has ever been brought down during that time. I believe I can support it with a good deal better spirit than any budget which has been submitted to parliament since 1921. Like the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) I regret very much that the government has seen fit, in a way, to reduce the special taxes for war revenue purposes. I think those taxes should be kept up as long as it is necessary to meet our war expenditures because personally I have not very much use for war. So long 1 a.m. as people feel they must pay for wars the less likely they will entertain any desire of supporting future wars if they can help it.
The Finance minister stated that the national debt at the present time amounts to $2,417,437,6S5. That is quite a large debt. Heretofore we have never made, any provision for the reduction of our national debt. All that we have done is to take the surplus we might have at the end of the year and apply it in reduction of the national debt. I think the time has come when we should make profusion for the reduction of the national debt, and that provision should be included in the budget. There should be an item of expenditure in the estimates to cover

The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
the actual reduction of our national debt, and personally I will not feel satisfied that we are handling that situation effectively until such provision is made. It is not enough to depend on the surplus each year for the reduction of that debt.
There is one omission in the budget which is rather surprising to me and that is that the Minister of Finance did not forecast the revenue for the coming year. I am quite ready to admit that it is a hard thing to forecast revenue, and any Minister of Finance who attempts to do it is more or less in the class of a prophet. But at the same time it gives a good deal of satisfaction to the people if they have some indication as to what the minister expects in the way of revenue for the coming year.
Referring to the income tax, I think it is now on a basis where it should be kept for some years to come unless something extraordinary happens. I would not like to see the income tax any further reduced, except perhaps in the lower incomes. As far as the higher incomes are concerned I think they should be kept as they are, because after all is said and done the people who have the income are those who should be the most heavily taxed, and the income tax in my judgment is one of the fairest taxes that we have. A good deal has been said with reference to the favourable balance of trade, namely to the extent of $402,000,000. The Prime Minister this afternoon referred to the fact that the balance of trade in Canada's favour was greater than the balance of trade in favour of the United States in her national trade, namely $402,000,000 for Canada and $352,000,000 for the United States. One thing which we must take into consideration is the fact that Canada is a debtor nation. We are paying out interest charges each year, and consequantly in order to meet those charges, we must export goods. That is the only way we can pay our interest charges and our debts abroad. By reason of the fact that we are a debtor nation it is necessary to be a tremendous exporter of goods to meet obligations incurred for what we import. The United States is a creditor nation, and consequently, because of that fact, she does not have to export a surplus of goods to pay for any liabilities she may have abroad. As a matter of fact the time is coming when we may expect the United States to have a balance of trade against her, on account of the payment of debts due to the United States.
The Prime Minister seemed to think that a good deal of this balance of trade was due in large measure to the methods of the govfVlr. Gardiner.]
ernment. There may be something in favour of that proposition, but do not forget that the people who make prosperity in this country possible, and who make it possible to have a balance of trade of $402,000,000, are the people who take off their coats and produce the wealth of the country. If the people of Canada had not been industrious, more particularly in our agricultural section of Canada, we would never have that favourable balance of trade, but we must always remember that any favourable balance of trade or any method of paying our liability can only be secured by producing goods and rendering service.
There is one item I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance and to the government regarding our obligations abroad. At the present time Canada has no means of telling how much we owe abroad by way of liabilities or debt. I think it would be quite possible for the Bureau of Statistics to secure the information, and if we had it we would be in a position to know just how our trade balances stood. We may not be exporting enough goods at the present time, even allowing for the surplus we have had during the last year to pay our liabilities abroad, and if that is the case we should be in a position to know it and be able to tell how much we have spent by way of surplus to meet the liability. It seems to me the Bureau of Statistics should be taken care of to a greater extent than it is at the present time. I do not think they have been given the opportunity to obtain as much information as they might have, and there is much information we should have from that bureau which we have not got and which would be of great value in future in determining our future policy.
The Minister of Finance in his closing remarks made a statement I think we all approve of. He pleaded' for unity in Canada, and in that I agree with him, but let me say there can be no unity in Canada so long -as injustices remain in this country. The only method whereby we -can secure unity is to see that justice is rendered to all sections of Canada ; when that is done we will have that unity which is so much desired by all classes of the country.
Since this session opened our bon. friends to the right have been very much perturbed about the farmer and have expressed themselves very freely as to his condition. They maintain that the farmer is not receiving justice under present conditions, and they are quite right. But Itihey propose, in order that the farmer shall receive a greater measure of justice, to place a higher protective duty on

The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
farm products. That is their remedy and the only remedy they propose, so far as I have been able to gather up to the present time. Let us see where the farmer would stand under a protective system. Let me remind hon. members first of all that very nearly fifty per cent of the population of Canada depends wholly or indirectly upon agriculture. How has protection treated the farmer in the past? It is only necessary to look over the statistics carefully (to ascertain how the farmer stands under a protective system. In 1923 I went to a good deal of pains to find out how the farmer stood, and after the investigation I made I felt that the farmer was robbed at the point of exchange. That is to say, when he came to exchange the products of his labour for the products of the factory he was robbed, because he did not get a fair exchange; so much so that, taking into consideration the prices as they were at that particular time, 1923, the farmer had to incorporate in his products approximately two and a half hours of labour in exchange for one hour of factory labour. Under those circumstances no agricultural section of Canada can be prosperous. I do not think it is quite as bad to-d)ay, on account of the fact that the price of farm products have risen quite substantially during the past two years. There is also a greater degree of prosperity among the farmers than there was in 1923. But notwithstanding the increased price of products the farmers to-da,y are not receiving equitable treatment when they come to exchange those products for the things they require. That is readily understood when you examine the situation.' As has been stated on many occasions, we farmers buy in a protected 'and sell in an open market at world's prices, because we export large surpluses of farm products. Under our fiscal policy the manufacturers can control to a large extent the prices of the commodities they sell, and by reason of that fact the farmer is unable to compete with them in the interchange of products.
Our Conservative friends have been assiduous in trying to cultivate the affections of the farmers. Now let me say this: I do not care how high the tariff may be on agricultural products. The fact is that just so long as the farmers sell individually and compete one against the other, not only in the home market but in the markets of the world, just so long will they be absolutely at a disadvantage under protection. Unless, therefore, the farmers realize that their only hope is in selling co-operatively, then under no circumstances can they expect to be prosperous in a country in which there is a protective
tariff. Let me give the experience of Australia. I have gone to the trouble to find out just what the situation is there and I think the House will be interested to follow the trend of events in that dominion. Some time ago as the result of a general election the Australian people found themselves face to face with a situation very much the same as we have here at the present time. No party had a majority in the House and none could carry on except upon a basis of cooperation. There were three different groups in that parliament, one of which was the fanner party. This party made an alliance with the high protectionists, two of the farmer representatives going into the cabinet. Eventually they had to accept the protective policy of the group with the largest following who had formed the government. That government increased the customs duties and in the long run the Australian farmer demanded protection for himself. And he was protected. The result is that to-day in Australia there is a two-price system in connection with the sale of farm products. Consideration is first given the requirements of home consumption, and what is left is of course exported. Take for instance the sugar cane industry. They can tell exactly how much sugar is produced, and I am informed that during the last year it required about 60 per cent of the sugar cane grown in the dominion to provide for home consumption. 40 per cent being exported. What happened? The cane growers received $12 per ton for their product on that portion consumed at home, while on the 40 per cent which they exported they received only $3 a ton. I may remark here that there is in Australia a Labour Arbitration Board, and the moment the prices of farm products went up under that system, owing to the fact that the farmers were in control of prices in the home market, the workingmen demanded a higher wage. They went to the board, pressed their case and got an increase. What happened again? Up went the prices of farm products. So in Australia they are afflicted with this vicious circle. And that is what will happen in Canada if the policy advocated by the Conservative party is put into effect and the farmers ever control the selling of their own products.
Our friends on many occasions have brought to the attention of the House the fact that the farmers of the United States have high protection, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has said more than once that when he comes into power he will erect a protective wall brick for brick with the United States. One would naturally think

The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
that the protective tariff in the United States should have operated beneficially to the farmers, but as a matter of fact it has not, because of the fact, as I have pointed out, that they compete one against the other in selling their products. What is happening in the United States at the present moment? The farmers are telling the government quite frankly that it. has fooled them on the question of the tariff, and they are demanding that congress set aside $375,000,000 for the purpose of taking care of the exportable surplus of farm products in the United States, in order that this surplus may be taken off the market, leaving the farmers in a position to increase the price of the product to the home consumer. That is the position the farmers are in to-day in the United States, and I understand that congress is thinking seriously of applying that suggested remedy. Under the circumstances it strikes me as folly for the farmers of Canada to accept the policy laid down by the Conservatives. I admit that if we were selling all our products through one channel a protective tariff would be a fine thing, for we could then take advantage of it. But the fact is that we cannot and until such a co-operative organization is actually in operation we shall not be able to do so.
A good deal of criticism has been made with reference to the reduction of duties on automobiles. The only fault I have to find is that it is not great enough. I should like to see a further reduction made in these duties, and in. my opinion, judging from the profits which I have seen that these companies make, if a further substantial reduction were made the manufacturers would still be left with sufficient protection. It is rather amusing to hear our friends discussing the motor industry. One thing that has struck' me more forcibly than any other in this connection is the fact that not one of these gentlemen seems to know anything about the industry, for there is not a practical motor man in this House. Most of the arguments are based on supposition and supposition alone, and just so long as that sort of debate goes on it will be impossible for us to know what the actual facts are in relation to the motor industry in Canada. Some time ago, as we all know, there was a delegation here from the city of Oshawa and surrounding towns to interview the government with a view to securing the restoration of the reduced duties. Having given the question careful consideration I have come to the [DOT] conclusion that quite evidently there is an understanding between employers and employees in eastern Canada 
that while they can get a high duty on whatever commodities they manufacture, they are in position to exploit a large section of the Canadian people. And they are quite willing to carry on that exploitation if they can. It seems to me that this delegation was here merely for the purpose of securing from the government the privilege of exploiting the masses of the Canadian consumers for another period of time. That is how it strikes me at any rate. Under the circumstances I am glad that the government reduced the duty on motor cars, and, I repeat, I would have been ready to support a still greater reduction had they had the courage to propose it. I have heard it rumoured. I do not know with what truth, that the higher officials of the General Motors Corporation of Canada do not even use the 'cars they manufacture in Oshawa, but bring in their cars from the States because of the fact that even after paying the duty they can get them cheaper. As I say, I do not know whether that is correct or not, but the rumour is so strong that it seems to me there must be some modicum of truth in it.
I think in some former debate I drew the attention of the House to this circumstance. We have natural resources in abundance, we have also machinery of production second to none in the world, and to supplement these we have a virile manhood willing to produce the things we require for our sustenance. Yet notwitstand'ing that fact we find a very large proportion of our population to-day is on the verge of want. Why is it that in a country so wonderfully endowed with natural resources, the machinery of production and a virile manhood, 25 per cent at least of our people are on the verge of the bread line almost all the time. That is the real problem before us. I do not think the fiscal question is the most important that we have to deal with. It does not make any difference whether you go to a highly protected country or to a free trade country, you find a similar amount of destitution in either. It seems to me we have been waiting a tremendous lot of time in dealing with the fiscal question instead of applying ourselves to the- one essential problem. \\ e should see to it that we get enough purchasing power into the hands of the consumers so that they can buy what we produce. In other words, it is a question of effective demand. When we have sufficient purchasing power then we will have an effective demand, and when we have an effective demand then all our industries will be running at full speed. And until we have that effective

The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
demand through increased purchasing power we can talk ourselves black in the face regarding free trade and protection and never accomplish anything worth while.
The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to-night made some reference to capital. He complained that under this 'budget people were selling their Canadian stocks and bonds and investing their money in Wall street in United States securities. I regret my hon. friend is not in his seat. I am afraid that he has not grasped even the first principles of economics. Had he done so he would not have made such a statement, for he is far too intelligent to make such an error. It is not possible for any great amount of money to be transferred from Canada to the United States or to any other country. We do not transfer money-we do not get money when new capital comes into this country. Money in the final analysis is merely a medium of exchange. It just measures values, or we express values by money. The only function of money is to facilitate the exchange of goods and services. We never export money unless we export bullion or gold when it is coined, and there is very little of that exported or imported. Now, what happens when we get new capital? For instance, if $200,000,000 of American capital comes into Canada it does not come in the form of American currency, because we do not allow that currency to circulate in this country. In the first instance that capital no doubt comes in by way of a 'bank credit, but just as sure as we get a bank credit of $200,000,000 of new capital from the United States, that will be followed by goods because that is the only way that capital can flow from one country to another. Some of our friends make the mistake of thinking that money is capital. Money is not capital. It never was and neve! will be. True, you can purchase capital if you have money, but money in itself is not capital. Capital is, for instance, factories, the machinery of production, raw material, and so forth; that is real capital, but money in itself is not capital at all. That is where many of our protectionist friends go wrong. For instance, our friends to the right say: You ought to treat capital a little better. If you would cut down taxes on capital we would get much more outside capital to develop our resources. But what about their high protective policy that they talk so glibly about? It is a direct tax on capital coming into this country because that capital, as I stated before, comes in in the form of goods, and those goods have to pay duty. Therefore our friends are very illogical in their reasoning. They want to see more capital come in.
All right, then cut down your customs duties and you will get capital more readily than under present conditions. That is the only way.
Our friends also seem to think that capital is of more value than labour; that is to say. they would give the preference to capital over labour. Let me give the House a quotation from Abraham Lincoln, which I think fits the situation exactly. This is what he said about capital:
Capital is the fruit of labour and could not exist if labour had not first existed. Labour therefore deserves much the highest consideration.
I quite agree with that. Greater consideration should be given to those who produce capital than to capital itself, and until we make up our minds to adopt that as our policy the workers of this country will be always shouting for higher tariff duties in order that they may be able to get work.

speechtext:
I do not care what he
was. I am merely quoting his opinion because it fits present-day conditions. It is not material to my argument whether he was a protectionist, a free-trader or a tariff for revenue man.
I would like to say a word about the Tariff Advisory Board. I am not satisfied in my own mind that this board is going to be worth anything; in fact, Mr. Speaker, I think that those who believe it will be of some value are more or less living in a fool's paradise. Let us consider the members composing the board at present, and see what business they are engaged in. One I understand to be a newspaper man, and also a politician; another is a boot and shoe manufacturer, while the third member is a farmer. I quite agree that if they look into the question of whether or not we should have a tariff on magazines coming into Canada, that member of the board who is a newspaper man will know something about it; he should, because that is his business. So far as boots and shoes are concerned, and as to whether we should have a higher tariff, a lower tariff, or no tariff at all, that member of the board who is a practical boot and shoe man will be able to give valuable information, and will know what he is talking about. In dealing with agriculture the third member will no doubt be able to give a good deal of intelligent service. But that, I think, is about all they are capable of inquiring into. When it comes to other industries such as the automobile industry, for instance, in all its ramifications,

The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
what hope is there of a board of that description being able to get an intelligent viewpoint of the whole circumstances? It would seem to me almost impossible under these circumstances for this board to function efficiently.
In connection with the tariff board in the United States, I would like to draw the attention of the House to one point. The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) referred to this board to-night and stated that our Tariff Advisory Board should have practically the same powers as that of the United States tariff board. That is, that they should have such power that if they find that the tariff should be raised or lowered, they may put that tariff into effect according to their judgment. I trust that that will never take place in this country. I think the representatives of the people, who are elected to this House to look after the public interest, should always keep control of the fiscal policy. I read an article the other day regarding the situation in the United States, where the board is composed of six members, I believe. Some time ago an application was made to that board to inquire into the sugar industry of the United States. That was done, and three members of the board thought the tariff should remain as it was, while three others, because of certain facts they had discovered. reported in favour of a lower duty. The board was deadlocked for some time and the report was not brought down for some twelve months. Eventually the administration tried to get rid of one or two of those members in favour of a reduction; they were offered all sorts of privileges and all kinds of high-salaried jobs, in order that the sugar trust might exploit the United States citizen by keeping a high tariff on sugar. I think such a condition is intolerable, and I do not believe the Canadian people would welcome it. However, I am quite willing to give this board an opportunity to function and we can then judge of its usefulness by the fruits of its labour.
I wish to make a protest, however. I suggest to the Minister of Finance and to the government that as far as I can see no provision is made for anyone to look after the interests of the consumers before that board. We can well understand that the individual consumer of farm implements, sugar or anything else, is not in a position to come before that board and plead his case. In consequence, then, if fairness is to be done the consumer as well as the industry under investigation, there should be a representative there to look after the interests of the consumers, and to see that all the facts are

brought forward. I would suggest to the government and more particularly to the Minister of Finance that a representative should be placed at the disposal of the consumers in order that their interests may be protected.
Now I have only one other subject to deal with, and I will be very brief. I would like to speak for a moment on the situation in the House of Commons as we find it at present. After the last general election we found that no party or group in this House commanded a majority, which meant that we either had to have another election, or that two or more of the groups must come together, carry on the government and allow parliament to function. That was done, and I have no regrets to express and no apologies to offer for the course of action I took. Our friends to my right have called us many different names; we do not mind that; we are used to it. But I would like to remind hon. members to my right that had we decided to throw in our lot with them the situation would have probably been reversed. Very little criticism can be levelled at us, therefore, for our action.
The point I would like to deal with to-night is more particularly our parliamentary institution as a whole. We must ask ourselves whether parliament is functioning as effectively as it might function, whether we are rendering the service to this country that we should render, and if not why not. Prior to 1921 we had' only two parties in this House, the Liberals and Conservatives. When the general elections were over one party was left with a majority in the House; they took up the reins of government and were responsible for the administration of affairs. The other party formed what was known as the official opposition, the 'leader of which received something like $10,000 a year over and above his indemnity. For what purpose? To oppose the government measures; to oppose everything the government brought down. The people, by a majority of votes, indicated that they wanted a certain party to form a government and to carry on the affairs of the country. But our politicians decided that something would be added, and that the other party would oppose all the measures the government brought down. That seems to me, Mr. Speaker, to be a ridiculous situation. There is one thing we must recognize. If you look over the industrial field you will find that co-operation is the order of the day, that co-operation is invading every industry in this country. Our parliamentary proceedings, in my judgment, are something like thirty

The Budget-Mr. Wilson (Vaudreuil)
or forty years behind the times, that is to say, behind our industrial development, and the time has come, in my opinion, when if this parliament is going to function under present conditions we shall have to have cooperation in politics just the same as we have co-operation in the industrial field. This parliament has been in session now for four months, and what have we done?

speechtext: Nothing; that is right. We have an insane system of doing the business of this country. If hon. -members of this House came to this House imbued with the idea that they were going to support measures, and not parties, we would have transacted the business that was to be done in this House two months ago. I care not what party may come into power; that is immaterial to me. But I do say this: This country is going to demand more from this parliament than what they have received in the past, and the time has come, unless we are going to run the risk of being laughed to scorn by the average person in Canada, when we must rearrange our method of doing business in this House, and I suggest as a remedy for getting away from our present conditions that all groups in this House try and co-operate for the purpose of giving the best legislation and the best administration that we possibly can to Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion on which I have risen to address this House. I have observed since the 7th of January when we met, that every hon. member who rose to speak congratulated you upon the position you occupy as Speaker of this House. I would rather congratulate the House and the people of Canada on having been able to obtain such a gentleman as yourself to occupy the Speaker's chair. I shall not enlarge upon your qualities, upon your ability, upon your savoir faire; it is too well known. But I see, and I believe my friends in this House also see, a different vision. They have watched you since this parliament opened. They have observed your patience, your impartial judgments, your knowledge, and they have sympathized with you in the great work that you have done since that day, and I think I am reflecting the opinion of everybody in this House and of the people of Canada generally when I say that they see a different vision, and that is, notwithstanding the great regret we should feel at your departure, we would like to see you occupy the position of Canadian representative at Washington. I have no
mandate to speak for you, Mr. Speaker, nor have I been inspired to make this remark, but, as the gentlemen on the other side of the House have so very correctly pointed out, we are one of the biggest customers of the United States, and I think it is about time that we had a representative at Washington to see that they become our customers as well as we being theirs. With your wide knowledge of affairs, with your manner, and I might add your lovely disposition, you would soon be able to bring down some of the bricks in that wall that at present stands between the two countries.

I shall occupy
a very few minutes, as I know the House is tired, and the people of Canada are also tired of this debate, which has lasted now for over a month. I shall therefore restrict my remarks to a few observations as a business man for the last fifty years in the metropolis of Canada.
For the information of the House and those who do not know me intimately-and I am glad for them-I may say that I happen to be interested in several industries in Canada and in several banking institutions; consequently I think I am in a position to make a few remarks on the questions that have come up in this debate. I shall not go into figures, for the figures that I have heard here in the last month would worry a dozen Philadelphia lawyers. I shall take the liberty, however, of giving you a picture as a business man, or as a layman, of what I have observed in this House since the 7th of January.
We were called to meet here on that day, and as you know, Mr. Speaker, it was rather dismal for this side of the House, and probably dismal also for the other side. Really it was not pleasant. I came here absolutely as an accident. Two weeks before nomination day I had no idea that I would ever occupy the honourable position I hold* in this House, but Providence decreed otherwise. When I came to this House on the 7th day of January, I tell you frankly, Mr. Speaker, I was absolutely bewildered. I never had any idea of the beauty and grandeur of this chamber. Much less had 1 any idea of the brilliant parliamentarians that sat in this House at that time and since. Frankly I have been amazed at the ability of some hon. members of this House. I had no conception that the House contained such able men as are in this House at the present time. I had no idea of parliamentary procedure: I had no

The Budget-Mr. Wilson (Vaudreuil)
idea of the number of precedents there are for the guidance of this House, and when I saw the volumes being brought in from the library, Mr. Speaker, from which hon. members quoted precedents going back three hundred or three thousand years, I tell you that I did not feel any higher or any bigger than Tom Thumb. I went to the Minister of Justice and offered him my resignation, but he declined to accept it. I want to say in all frankness that I had no conception of the knowledge or experience possessed by some hon. members of this House. I say to my friends on the street, in Montreal and elsewhere, to-day: If you think there is any sinecure in being a member of parliament, if you think that all he has to do is to walk into the chamber, you will soon discover that you do not amount to very much, and you will cease to criticize members of the House of Commons without knowing the facts as some people unfortunately do throughout this country.
Amongst the speakers that I have remarked, I might with the permission of the House mention a few names. We all know our Prime Minister, and his knowledge of technicalities. We all know our friend the Hon. Ernest Lapointe, who was so very patient throughout the month of January. We all know our friend Ed Macdonald, the popular Minister of National Defence. We all know our friend Mr. Cardin, the sympathetic Minister of Marine and Fisheries. We all know our friend the Hon. George Boivin. We all know the Hon. Charles Stewart, our new Minister of Labour (Mr. Elliott) and our Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon). We all know our friend the Hon. James Robb, who is very popular with the automobile people just now. Then there is the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning), that little dynamo from the west; and the Hon. Charles Marcil, of Bona-venture, that veteran member of the House whom we all admire. speechtext:
These fellows behind here happen to know what business I was in. Well, I have made a sfanfy of agriculture during that time, being honorary president of the Agricultural society of Vau-dreuil, as well as honorary president of the Agricultural society of Soulanges. I know the good people that live along the Ottawa and St. Lawrence and I can assure the House that my county can boast the finest inhabitants that are to be found1 anywhere. As I say, I have made a study of conditions from door to door and I modestly claim to understand the requirements of the farmers in my constituency, which I have no doubt is pretty much like any other district in the Dominion. Now, as a result of my observations I think that what the farmer requires to-day above everything else is cheap money. He must borrow at a lower rate of interest than he has been paying if he is to succeed1. We cannot expect him to pay 7 and 8 per cent and be able to carry on under those conditions. If he is to pay such rates of interest it will be impossible for him to buy the adjoining farm or a farm within a few acres of his own upon which to establish his son or sons. The great trouble has been that the farmer has had to pay altogether 
too much in the way of rate of interest. He cannot bear up under this load, nor will he foe able to throw off the yoke unless we can help him to secure cheaper money. I claim, therefore, that the rural credits bill is the most important piece of legislation that has ever been submitted to this House and it calls for the most careful consideration.
On the order paper I asked the question whether the government will provide in the rural credits legislation that borrowers under the ten-year period shall pay not more than 5 per cent on their loans, and those borrowing for a longer period than ten years, not more than 4^ per cent. I certainly do not think that farmers who borrow from the Dominion should be asked to pay more than 4J per cent. They cannot make both ends meet if they do. The government have not specified the rate of interest that will be charged, having left that question open; but when the matter comes up for consideration in due course I think that my labour friends and hon. gentlemen. of the Progressive party, as well as hon. members on both sides, should ask the government and the Finance minister to see to it that those provinces which take advantage of the $10,000,000 loan shall charge the farmer no more than 4 or 4| per cent for the money he borrows. Remember that the farmer with a family of eight, ten, fifteen of twenty children, such as we find in my county, pays these children nothing in the way of wages, and even then, notwithstanding the cry raised against the agriculturist about the prices he charges for his produce, he cannot make ends meet simply because of the extortionate rates of interest he must pay. In my opinion the solution would be for the government to borrow money at, say, 3 per cent. The banks to-day do not- pay more than \\ or 2 per cent on their deposits. I would ask my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) this question: Do the banks pay more than li or 2 per cent? The hon. member will not answer. To my mind 'he is the best posted man in this House on banking and he knows that the banks do not pay more than li or 2 per cent. And I will tell you why. The hon. gentleman is as foolish as a fox; he will not answer me. If you examine the statements of the banks you will find that two-thirds of the money on deposit is in the savings department at 3 per cent, while one-third is in current accounts bearing no interest. We may therefore discount that one-third, and that means that they pay 2 per cent. The banks do not pay you any interest if you deposit your money on the second or any

The Budget-Mr. Wilson (VaudreuU)
other date during the month; you must, deposit on the first, otherwise you lose your interest for the balance of the month. But when you borrow they charge interest from the moment you get the loan. It is not surprising, therefore, that the banks can put aside these wonderful reserves and pay their shareholders 10, 12, 13 and 14 per cent. No man knows better than I do that the banks now in Canada are as strong as the rock of Gibraltar; they are strong and powerful.
I know it, and I am proud of it. But I say that it is immoral that they should declare dividends of 12, 13 and 14 per cent to their shareholders. Any man should be content to have his money safe in their vaults and draw 6. 7 or 8 per cent. That is why the farmers are paying so much for their money, and I defy any accountant or any banker to stand up in this House or elsewhere and contradict the statement I have just made.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) the other night stated that when there was a financial crisis in his county the manager of a small local branch had to write to the home office in Toronto or Montreal before he could make a small loan to a client to finance the shipping of grain or cattle. Why should these branch managers be restricted to that extent? It is simply because they are limited to a certain amount in each of these branch banks, whereas the large deposits held by the banks are sent to New York on what they term "call loans." In 1907 I happened to be in the city of Calgary when that terrible financial crisis took place, and out of sixteen or seventeen banks only one or two would lend to any of its customers. The managers had received telegrams from their home offices, either in Toronto or Montreal, to refuse advances to any person. I met a man in Calgary that day whom certain hon. members know, and one of the biggest merchants in the west, and I had to assist him in a small way because he could not get any money from his bank. I ask my friend from St. Lawrence^St. George (Mr. Cahan):	Where was the money? It was in
New York with the gamblers. Millions of Canadian dollars are sent down to the gamblers there, thus depriving our trade and industry of the money it requires.
I am not trying to make a speech to the gallery, I am just giving my impressions as a business man. I am talking of a subject which I understand, and I defy any banker to contradict me, although he may not like what I am saying. Why this timidity in the House of Commons about our banks? Why is the question of banking not broached by 14011-225
my friend across the way, the ex-Minister of Militia (Mr. Mewbum), one of our old loves? He understands what I am talking about. We are not attacking the banks. As I understand it, we are a big family representing the Canadian people. We are not attacking the banks, we are in a sense working as a close coiporation in the interests of the people generally, and if we help the banks they should help us. I am giving the House tonight what to my mind is a solution of our banking problem. We must not allow the banks any more than we allow the railroads to go ahead without proper regulation, and without letting them know that we in this House understand the situation just as well as they do.
