speechtext:
I am not worrying. My hon. friend can ask me any question he likes. I am talking on a very serious subject. As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, my bank made me walk my room for months although my statement showed a growing increase. When I told one of my friends the situation I was in and that I would have to go into bankruptcy unless my paper was discounted as it usually was, but owing to the stringency of the money market my bank could not advance me any more money, having made large loans elsewhere in other quarters, he advised me, as I say, to get into my bank much deeper. This I did. Then I slept while the bank did the walking.
I know my friends opposite would be very much disappointed if I did not deal with one

3542	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Wilson (Vaudreuil)
item of the budget-the income tax. I believe our friends across the way would have raised the roof with their applause if one of their number had been able to bring down the budget of our Minister of Finance. It is easily seen by everybody that the new income tax provision is intended to reach wealthy individuals-there is no doubt about that-wealthy individuals who have so far succeeded in evading the surtax and the super tax by incorporating themselves into joint stock companies and only paying the corporation tax of 10-t per cent. They will now have to pay from 30 to 50 per cent upon their dividends. The double taxation, that is, the corporation now pays upon its profits 9 per cent, and the dividend owner pays his tax-there is where the howl comes in. Let us see how it works out. To-day the corporation pays one-seventh less than under the old tax, consequently it can now pay 8 per cent to its shareholders instead of 7 per cent. These facts are absolutely uncontradictable. My friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) knows that the corporations are paying one-seventh less; consequently they can pay one per cent more to their shareholders and still come out the same as before. I admit the big man over $10,000 will pay more, and that is the man we are after. Unfortunately I happen to be one of the greatest victims of that law, I am glad to say. I do not think many men in this House will be affected as much as I will be affected by this attack which the Minister of Finance has introduced into this House, but I am willing to make the sacrifice for the state, and I hope my hon. friends opposite will do the same, remembering that those sacrifices are only temporary. We are only lending the money to the government and from what I can see, if we remain members of parliament we will get it back. When the election was announced they came and asked me to save the country; two Liberals were running, and they were afraid a Conservative would step in and win out. A deputation of about 5,000 people, including many Conservatives, asked me to run. I capitulated and here I am. They said, "Come along; the election won't cost you a cent." I am reminded, Mr. Speaker, of two men in a county not far from my own who were selected as candidates, one for each party. They were neighbours, and one said to the other, " Baptiste, how much did you get from the party?" Baptiste said, "$3,000; how much did you get?" The first man said, " $3,000. We would be fools to spend this money; let's get into the same buggy and go round and shake hands with everybody and save our [Mt. L. A. Wilson.]
money." So they started out, and when they got to a certain part of the county they asked how it was going, and the answer was, " Oh, very doubtful, very dangerous; if you don't spend money you will both be beaten."
For the edification of my good friend the exMinister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) I would like to give one example which applies to all the figures which may be mentioned in regard to income tax. Surtax and supertax are paid, under the old law, only when above 15,000. If a corporation shows a dividend income of $10,000, under the old law the tax would amount to $115, leaving a net income of $9,885. According to the new tax the increased dividend amounts to $100, with a tax of $262, leaving a net income of $9,838, or a difference of about $46, so why should any howl be made?
The hon. member for West York stated in his brilliant speech that:
If the average Canadian income from dividends of Canadian companies was $7 000, the government would receive $S,750,000 more than last year, and if the average was $10,000 the extra collections would be $12,500,000.
This is just what the Minister of Finance wants; this is just what the government wants, and what the people of Canada want; they want to reach the millionaire, and they are doing so. The hon. member forgot to say, however, that the dividend holders would now receive more from their corporations, and the government will receive less from the corporations. The excess revenue that he mentions will be sliced off the millionaire's melon, and I will have to contribute my slice. I am bound to admire the ex-Minister of Finance; he is a great artist and can paint a most dismal picture or a most brilliant picture, as circumstances demand. The dividend owner now pays exactly the same tax as the salaried or business man, although the dividend owner does not work for his money. The majority of investors are wage earners, professional and unincorporated business men, and this scheme affords great relief to the bulk of Canadian workers and small investors.
Now, gentlemen, I have here clippings from a hundred newspapers. I will not read them all, but there are one or two which I think are important.
Mr. Robb's objective is obvious: he is directing his main attack against the larger private incomes and "unearned increment'' derived from invested capital, and plans to afford some alleviation to the recipients of smaller salaries and wages. The theory of his plan is just and has the support of almost every class, including those adversely affected...
"For some time past many wealthy individuals have successfully evaded the heavy assessments of surtaxes and supertaxes by the simple expedient of incorporating themselves and paying only the "corporation tax" of

The Budget-Mr. Wilson (Vaudreuil)
10-1/2 per cent. The revenue from these private corporations probably ran far in excess of their living requirements, and the owner would draw down in dividends or salary only enough to cover his expenditure, and on this amount only would he pay tax, at the usual rate for individuals...
And so on.
"Those in receipt of salaries and wages which are declared to government by their employers have never had any possible means of evasion and have undoubtedly, proportionately, borne the brunt of income taxation in the past. They are now given a considerable measure of relief by the increase in the amount of statutory exemption and in the low scale of taxation governing lower amounts...
I have hundreds of extracts of that kind which I will not read. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been very courteous to me tonight, but in conclusion I wish to say something regarding concealed bonds and securities. I want to impress upon the Minister of Finance that there are concealed bonds, coupons and securities hidden away in strong boxes throughout this country, not paying their honest taxes to the government. I want to say on the floor of this House that I believe some people are concealing their securities, bonds and coupons payable to bearer, and thus cheating this country of its just dues. These men are despicable; they should not be called Canadians, and I claim that the Minister of Finance, who has it in his power, should start the machinery to break into these strong boxes, if necessary, and make the owners of these concealed bonds pay what is due the government. I am not exaggerating when I make that statement. By what means can he do it? It is rather difficult to know. It is almost as difficult as to find out in the customs probe who is doing the smuggling-difficult when you get all sorts of people coming forward who will swear but not bet. I claim that the Minister of Finance and the government, who are striving by every means to increase the revenue of this country, should see to it that the man who is hiding coupon bonds and trying to defraud the government and the common people of this country who are earning their living by the sweat of their brow should be brought before the criminal courts of this country. How are you going to reach them, Mr. Minister? Reach them, if necessary, by printing a proclamation in the newspapers of this country stating that in the case of any man who conceals bonds and does not report his income therefrom in the regular way, when he dies and a statement of his affairs has to be made to the government of the province in which he lives for succession duties, his whole estate will be confiscated. That man will then start thinking of his family and pay his honest debts.
14011-225J
That is my advice, Mr. Minister, on that question, and I think in that way the treasury of this country would be the richer by several million dollars.
There is an hon. member of this House for whom I have a great admiration. I have not the pleasure of knowing him very intimately, but I have listened to all his speeches, and I consider that he is a very valuable man to the country, but like mosit great men he goes wrong sometimes. All great men have their weaknesses. I am now alluding to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). He stated in the House the other day:
I believe we are absolutely right in suggesting that after a certain exemption sufficiently large to enable a man's estate to provide for his immediate dependents, the rest of his estate ought to be very heavily taxed. Personally I would go a great deal further. I would say that it ought to be expropriated.
I do not know whether my hon. friend sent that out as a joker or not, but really it is a very serious thing. I have a high admiration for his ability; I am not trying to throw flowers by any means; that is not my style. Probably he is one of the most valuable men in this House, and we want men in this House like him and his colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I once belonged to the international union of labour myself. But the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would confiscate the capital or estate of a dead man. If that were done, what incentive would there be for a man to increase his capital after he had accumulated sufficient to provide for his immediate dependents? After making a certain amount of money by his ability, by his intelligence, and taking advantage of his opportunities, what incentive would there be for him to continue if all his surplus capital were to be confiscated? It would take the ambition out of a man, and I would point out to my hon. friend that the big financial men of this world who have accumulated large fortunes have done considerable good for their fellowmen. Take Mr. Carnegie, for instance, who happened to make three or four hundred million dollars. He did not carry the gold away with him when he left this world for a better. He did one of the greatest things in the world with his money. He established libraries all through the United States and Canada in any place that required one, to help in educating the people. Take Mr. Rockefeller's son; I happen to know him and the good work he is doing for humanity. Mr. Duke, of the American Tobacco Company, only a short time ago gave between forty and fifty
The Budget-Mr. Wilson

(Vaudreuil)
million dollars for hospital purposes. You gentlemen know what good the great kings of finance are doing with their capital, and remember many of these men came from the labour ranks. They are not men who have had a classical education. Carnegie, Henrv Ford and all these men had only the ordinary commercial education. I really fail to see why the hon. member should propound such a theory in this country. To me it sounds too much like Moscow or Russia, if I may say so, to be introduced in the House of Commons of Canada.
I shall not' detain the House for more than a few minutes longer. The other side of the House has been very kind to me. I can expect kindness from this side, because they are mostly old friends, but I appreciate the extreme courtesy and attention, numerical and otherwise, that has been accorded me. I have had some very great kindnesses extended to me since I came to this House on the 7th of January. I came here thinking I was a wonderful man, but I had not been here twenty-four hours before I found I was not in the picture. My friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) and a few other gentlemen were good enough to encourage me along by asking me to lunch, and I have now got sort of acclimatized. My friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) was also very kind to me, also my friend from East Hamilton Mr. Mewburn, and you, Sir, have also been very kind-and they have not touched me yet. I am going to tell you of the impression I had when I first entered this beautiful building. The first thing I saw when I came in by the Senate entrance was a big blackboard, with the word "Divorce." That was an awful thing to be staring one in the face. I got to the post office, and there I got a lot of printed matter from every department of the government, from the Minister of Agriculture, from the Minister of the Interior, from the Minister of Labour, and the Minister of Finance, informing me on international relations and how to kill moths in winter. I also received an envelope, with my address printed, advising me that there would be a caucus of the Liberal party at eleven o'clock. I thought that was wonderful. The attention given by the staff of the Sergeant at Arms of this House to hon. members is very satisfactory. You get stationery free, consisting of ink, pens, rubber, and pads of paper, maps, et cetera. I thought to myself when I came here first that I was in clover. I find they put me on several committees dealing with astronomy, botany and subjects of that kind,
I have commenced to feel very important.
[Ml. L. A. Willson.]
In conclusion I wish to say something about the railway question. I am sorry to disagree with my old friend of forty years standing (Mr. Maclean, York) on the railway question. My hon. friend wants a marriage of the railway systems of Canada. It is true there is a deficit on the Canadian National railway. The management show there is a surplus, but I do not believe there is any surplus at all. How can there be a surplus when all the members of this House get passes and travel free? I claim there has been a wonderful improvement on the Canadian National railways. There is no doubt about that. I travel on it every day and I have noticed the great improvement in the management of the line and in the deportment of the staff. I think Sir Henry Thornton is a wonderful railway man. He is working for love, I believe.

I would ask
my hon. friend to be discreet, and not give the price away. We have in Mr. Beatty a lovable man, trained under one of the greatest men who ever lived in this country and one of my oldest friends, Sir Thomas Shaughnessy. I pause to-night to pay a tribute to his memory. Under the tuition of Sir Thomas Shaughnessy Mr. Beatty learned the railway business and there are few better on this continent. Now, I believe in competition between these two systems. Allow them to be operated separately. If there is not competition between them you will not receive the attention or the satisfaction you are getting at the present time. This country is big enough to support two railway systems. Even though there should be a little deficit of twenty-five millions what does it amount to? The Canadian National Railways employ one hundred thousand people. One of the shops of the system is located in my own county and I know what an amount of good that railway is accomplishing. I know that the town of Coteau is dependent on the workshops of the Canadian National railway. If we consider that the one hundred thousand employees of the system have, on the average, families of three or four it means that half a million persons are dependent on the Canadian National railways for their bread and butter. Destroy that system, root it up, and it would cost you many millions more to support these people if you ever make an amalgamation with the Canadian Pacific. My advice is: Let Mr. Beatty and Sir Henry Thornton remain friendly enemies.
May I draw the attention of the House to the fact that in 1908 I sent a Christmas

The Budget-Mr. McKUlop
card to my friends, bearing the following poetic greeting:
Men should be judged not by their tint or skin,
The gods they serve, the vintage that they drink,
Nor by the way they fight or love or sin,
But by the quality of thought they think.
I happened to send one of those cards to a friend-the friend of both sides of this House -the then Prime Minister of Canada. The right hon. gentleman in question replied to me as follows:
Prime Minister's Office, Canada,
Ottawa, Dec. 20, 1908.
My dear Larry,
I received this morning your Christmas greeting and I will not lose one moment before sending you my thanks.
The ranks are getting thinner and thinner of the old friends who, in the early years of my career, urged me on, helped me and assisted me. You are one of them. To them and to you especially my heart goes with ever growing gratitude.
May the new year be to you a year of prosperity and happiness.
This is the wish of your old friend,
Wilfrid Laurier.
This shows the sentiment and the heart of a man we all respected and revered. Let us follow his example and harmony will reign forever in our beloved Canada.

The budget as brought down has dealt with only one industry in Canada. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would not
trespass on the valuable time of the House at this late hour, and indeed it had not been my intention until a very short time ago to say anything at all, but for the fact that after listening to the splendid address of the hon. member for Shel'bume-Yarmouth (Mr. Hatfield) last night, and having read some of it to-day in Hansard, I thought I would reply, however briefly, to some of the criticisms he levelled at some of the Maritime representatives in this parliament on the grounds upon which they conducted their campaign and upon which they were elected. As the hour is so late I will not discuss the point at any length, but I should like to quote just a sentence of what the hon. member had to say. For instance:
If my hon. friend will permit me to say so, this government has done the only thing done by any government to help Nova Scotia.
He went on to point out that the government had appointed a royal commission to investigate Maritime rights. Now the reason why there are so many representatives from the Maritime provinces on this side of the House is the fact that nothing has been done either by this or any previous government to assist either Nova Scotia or the other Maritime provinces. I make this statement in no partisan spirit, for the fact is that every parliament, Liberal and Conservative alike, has ignored the rights of the Maritime provinces. We feel that we have not received justice at the hands of confederation. On a former occasion on which I addressed the House I referred at some length to this question, and indicated why we Maritime righters, as we have been called, were elected. We were elected to press the claims which Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island justly have against the Dominion and which have been consistently ignored.
Just a word or two now with regard to the budget. I do not feel justified in supporting the budget. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), in presenting his statement, referred to it as a poor man's budget. I may be lacking in intelligence but I must confess that I cannot see in what respect this budget will be of any advantage to the poor man. Take for instance the reduction in automobile duties. Will that affect the poor man in any way? And when I speak of the poor man I am referring to wage earners whose income seldom exceeds $2,000. Are they interested in the purchase of automobiles? Take again the increased exemptions in income

The Budget-Mr. Quinn
tax: is that a matter of interest to the poor man? And the reduction in postage: to what extent does that affect the poor man's purse? The average workingman writes two letters a week. That is a matter of $1 spread over a period of twelve months.
I do not know that there is anything else the government can boatt about, apart from the slight reduction of 2J per cent in the sales tax on canned fish. This will mean very little to the average wage earner. Had the Minister of Finance been sincere the first thing he would have done would have been to eliminate altogether the 5 per cent sales tax which this government imposed upon the people; for that would have been of direct advantage to every man, woman and child in Canada. I leave that suggestion for his consideration.
Just before the budget was brought down I happened to read an editorial from the Labour Gazette from which I took the following quotation:
The tariff changes will lead to restriction of opportunities of employment without providing any commensurate benefit to the wage earner generally.
There is the opinion of the Labour Gazette. Further on, referring to the tariff board

and I call this particularly to the attention of the Labour representatives-the Gazette has this to say:
In the creation of the tariff board organized labour has been given no consideration, for there is no group in Canada whose interests are more vitally affected by the tariff reductions.
I am not going to say more, but I want to read to the House something which were it possible under the rules to do so, I would move by way of amendment to the budget. I know it is not in order to propose a second amendment, but if I could submit one it would be to the following effect:
That conditions in the Maritime provinces, especially with regard to employment and markets for basic products, such as coal and steel are at this very time alarming.
That as a consequence people are leaving for other lands in numbers unnaturally large.
That remedial measures have been already too long delayed.
That such conditions are due in no small degree to tariff reductions made in recent years, especially in respect of steel, which discriminate against the Maritime provinces.
And the House regrets that the budget of the minister of Finance contains not the slightest promise of relief.

speechtext:
In the space of just two minutes I want to say what in my opinion the policy of this government means to this Dominion. To my mind it is a tragedy that in this day and generation we should find in Canada a government, which is supposed to comprise the brightest minds in the country, utterly unable so to deal with our fiscal problem as to inspire the ordinary wage earners with confidence not only in themselves but in the country. Our people are leaving Canada for foreign shores to seek the employment which they are unable to find at home. It is most unfortunate that representatives of the Canadian government and representatives of our leading manufacturing industries, particularly of Ontario, including the producers of motor cars, should not find it possible to come together and decide upon a policy in the interests of the country.
I might mention again what I dealt with in some detail in the debate on the Address. The longer the Liberal party stays in power the more are we getting out of balance with regard to the number of our people engaged in the production of raw material as compared with those employed in the production of manufactured goods. Whereas in the United States every year more and more men are engaged in the various processes of manufacturing and a diminishing number are employed on rough labour, in this country the conditions are reversed. What is the reason? The United States consistently adheres to a protective policy, while under this government Canada is handicapped by an unstable tariff policy.
And the government has gone a step further. Under this budget the imposition of double income tax will discourage the investment of money in Canadian industries. This is another example of how the industrial life of the Dominion is being crippled by the ineptitude of this government.
